#4848. The puppy-sized bats of Madagascar are shrinking

Published Oct 29, 2026 10:00 AM EDT

It’s the stuff of nightmares. A bat the size of a large-breed puppy with five-foot-wide wingspans darting across the sky. But don’t worry. The giant flying foxes want fruit, not your blood.

However, biologists do have something to worry about regarding these enormous winged mammals. Madagascar flying foxes (Pteropus rufus) are shrinking. They have been getting smaller over the past several decades, which biologists suspect may be related to an increase in large-scale commercial hunting. A study published today in the Journal of Mammalogy details the findings.

While sifting through a collection of preserved flying fox skulls and skins at the Field Museum in Chicago, the study’s authors noticed that the specimens in the archive appeared larger than those they had seen during recent fieldwork in Madagascar. They were not sure why the modern bats were so much smaller than those previously collected.

“I was thinking about a million different angles to explain why the bats were getting smaller. I wondered if it was related to changes in temperature or habitat,” Emily Cornelius Ruhs, a study co-author and wildlife ecologist at the Field Museum’s Negaunee Integrative Research Center, said in a statement.

Ruhs spoke about this puzzle with her colleague and study co-author Steve Goodman, and he had a different idea in mind. These fruit bats are legally considered vermin in Madagascar, and are often associated with eating commercially important fruits. They are also a game species, and hunted for food at a large scale in parts of the island nation. Goodman, a full-time field biologist, has been living and working in Madagascar for nearly 40 years. After examining the late 18th and 19th century museum specimens, he noticed that many were a “monster size” compared to the animals handled in the wild today.

“Hence, the idea was formed that they have diminished in body size as a result of recent heavy hunting pressure and they are not living as long as they did in decades past,” Goodman added. “This underlines the importance of historical museum material in helping scientists to understand change through time.”

To investigate further, Goodman visited the nine natural history museums across the United States and Europe. He examined 121 Madagascar flying fox specimens collected over the past 150 years, measuring the bat’s skulls and teeth. Ruhs then performed statistical analyses, to look for overall trends in size.

The team saw a clear drop in size beginning around 1980, when bat hunting likely became more commercialized. This change was so stark that Ruhs initially thought there must be a mistake.

“I thought that there must be something wrong with the analysis, there was no way that the rough estimate we had was correct, but it was,” Ruhs recalled.

While the study establishes a correlation between the bats shrinking and the commercialization of hunting, the team is not not explicitly showing that the commercialized hunting over 40 years caused the bats to shrink. But Ruhs suspects that it’s not a coincidence that the largest bats were the ones that were disappearing.

“If you’re the biggest bat in the sky, you might be the easiest target. You’re also going to provide a hunter with the most meat,” said Ruhs.

Additionally, many of the largest flying foxes in this study were older individuals. So if bigger, more mature bats of breeding age are being targeted by hunters, that could affect flying fox populations overall.

Targeting larger bats might not be the only factor in the trend towards smaller bats. Deforestation, climate change, human activity, and shifting timing of fruit season could be playing a role at the same time, and not one cause.

“These bats are an important food source in certain portions of the island for people to feed their families or on the menu in some roadside restaurants, so it is critical to figure out ways to protect the bat populations,” says Ruhs. “This needs to involve higher levels of protection following new national laws, particularly at breeding sites, so that the populations don’t collapse.”

#4847. Rivian (RIVN) Q3 2026 earnings: revenue up 38%, R2 now its best-seller

Rivian (RIVN) just released its Q3 2026 earnings, with revenue up 38% year-over-year to $2.155 billion. The R2, in its first full quarter of deliveries, is already the company’s best-selling vehicle, ahead of both the R1 and the Amazon van.

The results beat Wall Street’s expectations, and Rivian is raising its 2026 guidance on every metric. But the car business is still losing money, and the R2 ramp made the automotive margin worse this quarter.

We already had the volume side. Rivian reported earlier this month that it built 19,751 vehicles and delivered 19,248 in the quarter, both records. Deliveries were up 46% from a year ago and 58% from Q2.

Analysts were looking for about $2.02 billion in revenue, an adjusted loss of $0.61 per share, and an adjusted EBITDA loss of roughly $576 million, according to Bloomberg consensus. Rivian beat all three.

The demand signals for the R2 are good. Rivian says reservation conversion for the launch edition trim stayed above its expectations, it added a second R2 production shift in Normal, Illinois, and demo drives jumped to over 103,000 in the quarter, up from 57,000 in Q2.

The problem is the automotive gross margin. Rivian’s automotive segment posted an $80 million gross loss in Q3, a -5% margin. That’s better than the $130 million loss a year ago, but worse than the $36 million loss (-3%) we saw in Q2.

Rivian blames about $120 million of extra cost of revenue on the R2 ramp, compared to production at “more normalized levels.” And the quarter got help that won’t repeat on demand: $81 million in regulatory credit revenue and an IEEPA tariff refund receivable.

Strip out the credits and the automotive segment lost about $161 million at the gross level, or roughly $8,400 per vehicle delivered. Not great.

But there’s real progress under that. Rivian says automotive cost of goods sold per unit fell by more than $12,000 quarter-over-quarter thanks to the higher R2 mix and better fixed-cost leverage. Our own math from the filing puts it at about $84,700 per vehicle in Q3, down from $96,700 in Q2. Revenue per vehicle is coming down too, which is the point of a cheaper car: about $76,300 excluding credits, versus $85,000 in Q2.

The only reason Rivian posted a consolidated gross profit is its software and services segment, which brought in $605 million in revenue and $256 million in gross profit, a 42% margin.

Of that segment revenue, $354 million (59%) came from the joint venture with Volkswagen Group, which pays Rivian for electrical architecture and software development work. Rivian says it expects to recognize that revenue through about mid-2028. Autonomy+, the paid driver-assist package launched in April, is also in there, and Rivian says take rates are “trending ahead of our expectations.”

With 41,807 deliveries through September, Rivian needs between 25,193 and 28,193 in Q4 to land in the new range. That would be another record by a wide margin. Rivian is providing this guidance a month into the quarter, which gives strong confidence it will hit at leat the lower end of that target.

The capex cut is about “timing of spend,” not savings. Phase 1 of the Georgia plant, which is supposed to add 300,000 units of annual capacity for R2 and R3, is still under construction.

On cash, Rivian ended the quarter with $5.502 billion, or $7.095 billion in total liquidity once you add its credit facility and the $1 billion term loan Volkswagen funded in October. That’s after the $1.5 billion share sale in July. Free cash flow was -$1.124 billion in Q3 alone.

This is a good quarter for Rivian, and the R2 is clearly working. Becoming the best-selling Rivian within one full quarter, while the ramp is still early, is about as good a start as you could ask for. We saw the R2 roll off the line in April, and the demand side has held up since.

But be careful with the headline beat. A lot of it came from outside the car business: Volkswagen’s checks, regulatory credits, and a one-time tariff refund. The thing Rivian actually builds and sells lost more money at the gross level than it did last quarter.

Picked my R2 up a week ago and I’m already in love. It was worth the two year wait! I find myself looking for excuses to jump in and go for a joy ride.

Rivian is going to sell a metric ton of the lower cost versions.

The number we care about most is the $12,000 drop in cost per vehicle. If that keeps going as the second shift fills and the $120 million in ramp costs fade, the automotive segment can get to breakeven on its own. If it stalls, Rivian is a software contractor for VW with a money-losing car company attached.

I am betting on the former. With a shift added right before the quarter started, production will likely increase significantly in Q4, and Rivian already has strong visibility into demand a month into the quarter.

If anything, I’m impressed by the demand Rivian is seeing for the more expensive launch edition of the R2. It bodes well for the cheaper version, as long as it manages to get its cost down over the coming months.

#4845. Inside the Governor’s Mansions That Will Soon Be Home to 19 Newly Elected Leaders

In January, the United States’ 19 newly elected governors won’t just have inauguration day on their calendars, but moving day, too. All but five states have governor’s mansions for their leaders to live and work from, with the exceptions being Arizona, Idaho, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Vermont. These executive residences tend to be grand in style and scale, often possessing a long, rich history—even some haunted ones.

Sometimes, governors forego their official residences in favor of privately owned homes. For example, California governor Gavin Newsom recently listed the $7.5 million Fair Oaks home he lived in instead of the official executive residence, a 19th-century Victorian in Sacramento. Montana’s governor’s mansion is currently empty and in disrepair, while a governor hasn’t inhabited the official residence in Nebraska in over a decade.

Most states, however, have longstanding traditions of their leaders living in their official governor’s mansions. Virginia has the oldest continuously inhabited executive residence—every governor has lived there since 1813. If our new league of governors opts for tradition, here’s where they will be resting their heads for the next few years.

Republican Tommy Tuberville won Alabama’s gubernatorial race and will be able to move into a 119-year-old mansion in Montgomery following his inauguration. Built in 1907 by architect T. Weatherly Carter, the 17-room neoclassical residence features a row of four Corinthian columns at its front entrance, which opens to a foyer with a grand bifurcated staircase.

California’s new governor-elect is democrat Xavier Becerra, who will soon reside at a three-story Victorian in Sacramento. Built in 1877, the 20,000-square-foot house was thoroughly renovated in 2015, decades after Ronald and Nancy Reagan’s brief stint living there in 1967 before deeming it uninhabitable. The mansion was then used as a museum until its 2015 update, when it became home to the state’s governors once again. It has 30 rooms, Italian marble fireplaces, original wood floors, and a kidney-shaped swimming pool.

In Denver, democrat Phil Weiser will receive the keys to the red brick governor’s mansion known as Colorado’s Home. Built in 1908, it has been the state’s official governor’s residence since 1960. The Colonial Revival–style home has 27 rooms and shares its one-acre grounds with gardens, a historic gazebo, a greenhouse, and a carriage house. Thanks to John Hickenlooper, governor from 2011 to 2019, the home also has a rotating selection of local beers on tap.

Republican Byron Donalds just made history as Florida’s first Black governor. The state’s Greek Revival–style governor’s mansion in Tallahassee was completed in 1956 on the site of the original governor’s mansion built in 1907, which had fallen into disrepair. A screened swimming pool, a greenhouse, and a rose garden are among its amenities.

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms has the distinction of being the first Black woman governor-elect in the United States. Her soon-to-be residence in Atlanta is a 30-room Greek Revival mansion that was built in 1967 by architect A. Thomas Bradbury. Across three levels, it measures in at 30,000 square feet.

Iowa’s governor’s mansion, known as Terrace Hill, will soon be home to democrat Rob Sand. Dating all the way back to 1869, Terrace Hill is an 18,000-square-foot Second Empire–style residence in Des Moines where Iowa’s governors have lived since 1976. Its first two floors are open to the public as a museum and events space.

Democrat Hannah Pingree will move into the Blaine House in Augusta, Maine. Originally built in 1833 in a combination of Federal and Greek Revival styles, the mansion has been the state’s official governor’s residence since 1919, when renovations gave it a more Colonial style. It has 28 rooms across two stories, including a billiards room. The property also hosts a formal garden and a tennis court.

In Michigan, democrat Jocelyn Benson has the good fortune of governing a state with two official executive residences: one in the state’s capital of Lansing, and an official summer residence on Mackinac Island. The former is a 1957-built 8,700-square-foot ranch-style home with five bedrooms and four bathrooms; the latter is an Arts-and-Crafts-style mansion that was built in 1901.

Nevada also elected its first Black governor, democrat Aaron Ford, who will soon reside in a Classical Revival–style mansion designed by architect George A. Ferris in 1909. New Mexico’s governor-elect, democrat Deb Haaland, has made history as the first Native American woman to hold that title. In Santa Fe, the governor’s mansion is referred to as The People’s House. Designed by architect W.C. Kruger, the midcentury-modern structure was completed in 1955.

Democrat Amy Acton will be Ohio’s next governor, granting her residency inside a 1925 mansion in Bexley, just outside of Columbus. Marsha Blackburn, the Republican governor-elect of Tennessee, can move to a 10-acre estate in Nashville’s Oak Hill suburb. Republican Eric Barlow will soon have access to the governor’s residence near Frontier Park in Cheyenne, Wyoming. #4844. Permanent Daylight Saving Time is dangerous for kids, new research says

Published Oct 29, 2026 11:00 AM EDT

Daylight Saving Time (DST) has always been contentious. In the United States, the debate resurfaces almost as regularly as everyone shifts their clocks backwards in the fall and forward in the spring. Earlier this year, the U.S. House of Representatives even passed a bill called the “Sunshine Protection Act” to make DST permanent. However, the legislation hasn’t progressed much further since July, and we are mere days away from falling back.

That’s for the best, according to a team of biologists at the University of Washington, Seattle (UW). In a study published today in the journal Current Biology, researchers contend a permanent DST would needlessly endanger countless children around the country during their morning school commutes.

“Permanent DST would move the school day earlier relative to the sun without changing a single bell schedule, putting millions of children on streets and at bus stops in the dark for weeks or months every year,” said study co-author and UW chronobiologist Horacio de la Iglesia.

De la Iglesia and his colleagues explained that while most DST chatter centers on how much light is available during evening hours, it ignores the early morning consequences. Most children in the U.S. return home from school before sundown with or without DST, but a permanent shift could make predawn commutes a regular occurrence around the country. According to de la Iglesia’s team, authors of the Sunrise Protection Act didn’t factor in these issues before the school day when crafting their bill.

To investigate, researchers the team examined school start times in 14 states with a hypothetical permanent DST, then compared them to local sunrise times. They calculated roughly 356 million additional trips to school before sunrise. When expanded to the entire country, the authors estimate over two billion predawn school trips. From there, the study authors reviewed available traffic data to determine that dark mornings dramatically increase the chances of pedestrian collisions. Fatal instances involving individuals ages 5 to 18 are more likely during dark hours, too.

The ramifications aren’t concentrated in any single region of the country, either. Northern and southern states would all be affected, although Georgia would likely experience the most dark morning commutes in the nation. That said, permanent DST would negatively affect more children based on socio-economic lines.

“The burden of permanent DST is likely greatest for children who walk, wait for buses, or arrive early for school breakfast programs, which disproportionately serve lower-income families,” added UW biologist and study co-author Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante.

If the U.S. ever did pass a similar law, Ferrante and de la Iglesia argued that it should be for a permanent standard time (ST). That switch would reduce the current number of dark school mornings by half. A permanent ST is also more aligned with the biological and social clocks of children and adolescents.

“No clock policy adds a single minute of daylight. It only changes when that daylight is available,” said de la Iglesia. “Permanent DST moves an hour of light out of the morning, when children travel to school, and into the evening.”

But if all that somehow weren’t enough, the study’s authors contend that historical precedent should ensure the “Sunshine Protection Act” never sees the light of day, so to speak.

“The U.S. has tried this before,” said Ferrante, referring to a year-round DST that went into effect in January 1974.

The shift didn’t even last a year—in large part due to worries about children heading to school.

#4843. Toyota’s EV sales more than doubled in a year, but gas cars are getting crushed in China

Toyota’s EV sales have jumped 127% through September, but that isn’t telling the whole story. Slumping demand for gas and hybrid cars in China has pushed global sales lower for three months in a row.

Including Lexus, Toyota sold 309,766 battery electric vehicles (BEVs) globally through the first nine months of 2026, up 127.4% from the same period last year.

Except for January (+87.5%), Toyota’s EV sales have more than doubled every month this year compared with 2025.

The higher demand comes after Toyota and Lexus launched updated versions of their first-gen electric SUVs, the bZ4X (now the bZ in the US) and the RZ.

Toyota has added several new electric models, including the C-HR+ (C-HR in the US), bZ4X Touring (bZ Woodland in the US), and Urban Cruiser, while Lexus now offers the ES EV. Both brands will introduce a three-row electric SUV, which is expected to go on sale over the next few months.

According to data from Cleantechnica, the Toyota bZ4X became the 20th best-selling EV worldwide through August, with nearly 100,000 units sold.

While its EVs are catching on, Toyota Motor’s global sales fell for the third straight month in September.

Toyota sold 860,107 vehicles in September, down 2.2% from the previous year. The company said that although overall demand remained steady, sales in China fell, leading to lower overall sales than last year.

Through September, Toyota sold 7.51 million vehicles globally, down 3.4%. In China, Toyota’s sales plunged nearly 20%, marking its eighth consecutive month with lower sales.

Toyota said the overall market in China “remained weak due in part to rising gasoline prices, while the market for gasoline vehicles and hybrid vehicles was particularly affected,” resulting in lower sales.

In the first nine months of 2026, Toyota sold just over 1.05 million vehicles in China, 18.9% fewer than in the same period last year.

Toyota sells several electric vehicles through its two joint ventures (GAC Toyota and FAW Toyota) in China, including the bZ3, bZ3X, bZ5, and bZ7.

After the US, China is Toyota’s second-largest market. Through September, Toyota has now sold more vehicles in its home market of Japan (1.19 million) than in China.

To turn things around and compete with companies like BYD, Toyota, like many major OEMs nowadays, is increasingly adopting more Chinese EV tech and manufacturing practices.

Nikkei reported in August that Toyota plans to build a new Lexus electric SUV in China, rather than in Japan as it has traditionally. Production is expected to begin at Lexus’ new manufacturing plant in Shanghai next fall.

Toyota's EV sales still represent less than 3% of its overall sales. This is the real news.

BTW, Toyota's European sales got hit in a similar way. They are up 0,7% YoY but that's compared to a rising overall market of 5,7%. This lead to it's market share shrinking.

The new Lexus EV will use advanced manufacturing methods, including gigacasting, to cut costs and speed up production.

Toyota isn’t the only legacy automaker struggling to keep pace in China’s fast-moving automotive market.

Volkswagen Group CFO and COO, Arno Antilitz, admitted the company “must act quickly and decisively” after reporting third-quarter sales in China dropped 38% to 405,800 units on Thursday. The company also plans to use technology developed in China for its next-gen EVs, which it will sell overseas.

EVERYONE KNOWS THAT Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson are one of the great duos in show business. #4841. 12 Best Bar Carts to Elevate Your Entertaining Game (2026)

Bar carts are not just for someone who likes to host a cocktail soirée. In fact, the predecessor of the bar cart was once a Victorian-era tea trolley. Only when the Prohibition hit did these side tables on wheels find their true calling. Many, many iterations later—think: Alvar Aalto’s iconic tea trolley, which has inspired many picks on this list, and USM’s blessedly minimalist spin on the genre—the beauty of this booze trolley remains that it can completely transform a room or give a useless nook some purpose. Though they’ve fallen out of favor in many modern homes, these rolling wonders make an elegant—and functional—home base for all your mixology essentials, from stemware and decanters to liquor bottles and mixers. They also don’t have to be used to haul booze at all, instead doubling as portable storage for crafts, books, beauty or bathroom supplies, and houseplants.

Employed outside, a stylish bar cart can give a dinner party some polish or emulate a poolside butler. Load it up with a pitcher of lemonade and a basket of sunscreen on top, and extra towels on the bottom and you’ll never have to leave your lounge.

Made of solid and veneered walnut with elegant brass details, the Cotu (from the makers of our favorite bar cabinets) is a delightful midcentury-style bar cart that has a distinctive asymmetrical incline on each shelf. Use the wider edge for housing smaller utensils and glasses, while leaving the shallower end for larger bottles that are less likely to topple over the edge.

Birch Lane’s Reinhart cart speaks to farmhouse design, especially in this punchy shade of blue. Turned legs give the overall look a polished appearance, but scalloped paneling on the top shelf and a fun hue ground the piece in something that’s suitable for more playful design aesthetes.

Think of the Wallace Serving Bar Cart as the anti-bar cart. The wooden design resembles a sleek-looking side table thanks to its grounded base, but underneath, a discreet set of wheels gives you the ability to roll the decor piece anywhere a gin and tonic or negroni needs mixing. Its clandestine silhouette also allows it to double as a shelf for non-drink making goods like magazines, coffee table books, or your favorite potted plants.

While this circular cart might lack ample space for large-scale barware, its Art Deco style gives it an Old Hollywood feel. Placed in an area that gets lots of sunshine, the amber tempered glass shelves diffuse a warm glow, layering in some unexpected coziness during cloudless days.

Business & Pleasure Co.’s Al Fresco bar cart is a throwback to a time of leisure under the Parisian sun. While the cart can be used indoors, we can’t imagine a better place for it than on a terrace surrounded by a garden. As if the charming scalloped trim wasn’t enough, the designated umbrella hole nails the summery vibe for poolside mojitos or curbside lemonade stands.

To find that heirloom quality of Victorian design lore, look no further than Greenrow’s Liona bar cart with Barley twist legs to charm you an dyour guests. The two shelves in a chestnut finish offer ample space for glassware and a floral arrangement, should you want to create a whole spread for summer spritzers.

Here’s a piece of decor with lots of Mad Men energy. With its sloped legs and clean-lined silhouette, this cart has enough midcentury-modern charm to appeal to retro design lovers. Two full-size shelves have ample room for old fashioned and martini ingredients, while a mid-tier half shelf can either support a few extra bottles or a stack of your favorite mixology books.

For studio apartment dwellers or homes where square footage is precious, this miniature cart is slim enough to slip into discreet spaces until happy hour rolls around. Made of sturdy beech wood, rounded edges and a light hue soften the beverage cart’s overall look. We think these elements also make it well-suited for adorning Scandi- or Japandi-centric spaces.

Leather accents, exposed wood grain shelves, and an antiqued gold finish bring a polished look and feel to this spacious bar accessory. Two levels with a generous amount of clearance makes it easy to style, whether you’re packing it full of bottles or prefer a more curated decor approach of sculptural glassware.

With storage for four wine bottles, you can stock multiple kinds of sippers, from sparkling to organic, to please even the snobbiest of guests.

#4840. Rivian’s electric van gets 30% more range and AWD, now delivering

Rivian has started delivering the first major hardware upgrade to its electric van since production began in 2021: a bigger LFP battery pack good for 30% more range, and a new dual-motor AWD version.

The company confirmed in its Q3 2026 shareholder presentation that deliveries of the new variants began in early October. That’s the first real spec bump for a van that has been stuck at about 160 miles of rated range for years.

Rivian first mentioned the upgrade in its Q4 2025 letter, which we covered in February when Amazon’s fleet of Rivian vans grew 50%. At the time, Rivian only said it was “developing” a larger battery and AWD to “expand EDV route coverage” in Amazon’s network.

Now it’s shipping. In today’s presentation, Rivian says the new variants are “specifically designed to expand route coverage into more rural networks,” with the AWD configuration and the bigger pack offering “a 30% increase in range.”

EPA certification documents for the 2027 EDV 700, issued September 17, list the new pack at 129 kWh usable. Rivian has marketed the current van with a 100 kWh LFP pack, so that’s roughly 29% more energy, which lines up with the 30% range claim.

The upgrade is limited to the bigger 700 van, the one with 652 cubic feet of cargo space. The smaller 500 keeps its existing pack and front-wheel drive.

The EPA filing gives unadjusted lab range figures, which always run high because they skip the correction for real-world driving:

Rivian rates the current 700 at “up to 160 miles.” Apply Rivian’s 30% to that and the new FWD van lands around 208 miles. Using the AWD van’s smaller 23% gain from the EPA tests, we estimate the dual-motor version at about 195 to 200 miles.

So AWD costs roughly a third of the range gain. For a van, that’s a fine trade. Rural routes mean longer distances between stops, plus gravel, mud, and snow, which is exactly where a front-wheel-drive van with a full load of packages in the back struggles.

200 miles is roughly what Rivian promised for the van when deliveries to Amazon started in 2022, before the rated figure settled closer to 160 miles. Rivian is finally there, four years later.

The timing helps on the sales side too. Rivian’s van business is still overwhelmingly Amazon, years after the exclusivity period ended in late 2023. We spotted a Rivian van in Walmart+ livery on a car hauler in Indiana just this week, though neither company has announced a deal.

The competition has also thinned out. GM ended BrightDrop van production in Ontario and Canoo went bankrupt, leaving Ford’s E-Transit as the main full-size electric alternative in the US.

Rivian needs to make the sales to USPS. I am starting to see those vans all the time now. It looks like it is designed from ground up to optimize for delivery. Extra height for drivers, lower floor of entry, great visibility in the front. Low bumper and lower headlight position for safety. Overall, great design.

Too bad that GM dropped Brightdrop van just as they are getting popular. I see a lot of FedEx trucks are now Bright drop. Perfect timing when diesel price is thru the roof. GM never have the long term view and always good at starting something but give up just before it becomes a hot seller.

This is the upgrade the van needed. 160 miles was always fine for dense urban Amazon routes, but it boxed Rivian out of a big chunk of the fleet market: rural delivery, utilities, telecom, anyone who can’t guarantee a short loop and an overnight charge.

Getting to around 200 miles real-world, with AWD as an option, opens a lot of those routes. And unlike most of the EV van market right now, Rivian is actually building and improving its product rather than killing it.

The question is whether Rivian can turn that into customers other than Amazon. A Walmart+ wrap on a car hauler is a nice sign. We’d want to see a real order. If you’re running a fleet and these specs change your math, we’d love to hear from you.

#4839. Extremely chill bear named Paul wins a Dude-approved award

Published Oct 29, 2026 12:09 PM EDT

Like people (and snowflakes), no two bears are alike. Some have their own innovative fishing styles, or “walk on water,” while others will even adopt cubs who are not their own. And a bear named Paul is known for his patience. Paul lives in southeastern Alaska, where he spends his summers catching fish in Anan Creek. He is also the winner of the 2026 Dude abides Award from the United States Forest Service team in Tongass National Forest.

According to the team, Paul exhibits the patience and nonchalance of The Dude, an extremely chill character from the 1998 film The Big Lebowski. Brought to life by Jeff Bridges, The Dude’s catchphrase “The Dude abides” is the final line of the movie, and what inspired this award.

“Paul chose kindness over combat when his fish were stolen,” the team writes. “This bear was seen with a fish in his mouth more frequently than without, and opportunistic rivals with lesser skills in fishing liked to steal his catch.”

Anan Creek is home to one of the largest salmon runs in the world, so defending all of his catches is a waste of energy. As a result, Paul abides, since fishing is more rewarding than fighting.

Paul is known for two thin lines on his chest with a scar on his left ear and won the award for pickiest bear in 2024.

The U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest are currently doling out the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Tongass National Forest.

The nation’s largest national forest, Tongass covers most of Southeast Alaska, including the capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 known bears feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears (Ursus americanus) and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Like their counterparts further north in Katmai National Park, the bears return annually each summer to eat salmon and teach their young how to fish and survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear and explore.org’s cameras also broadcast live streams of their antics.

#4838. A Guy’s Guide to the Many (Many) Dick Myths of 2026

A urologist right-sizes the manhood myths that have recently sprung up online.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

From biohacker Bryan Johnson to looksmaxxer Clavicular, every influencer claims to have the secret to looking bigger, getting harder, and lasting longer. “Penis-maxxing can run the gamut,” says Rena Malik, MD, a urologist, sexual health expert, and Men's Health advisor. “It's a huge market.” (Pun probably intended.) Do any of their tactics work though? The jury is out, but the doctor is in: “I want people to think about the long-term health of their penis, not just right now,” Dr. Malik says, which is why she wrote a whole book about it (The Hard Truth, out now). Here, she right-sizes the manhood myths that have recently sprung up online.

Sometimes (note: not “often”), the ingredients in these supplements do work for some men (note: not “all”—or “many”). That could be because of L-arginine and L-citrulline, ingredients that increase nitric oxide and allow more blood to flow to the penis, says Dr. Malik. Or it could also be the placebo effect.

The supplement industry is largely unregulated and many products have little to no scientific backing. Some supplements even contain contraband PDE5 inhibitors, like tadalafil and sildenafil, or animal testosterone. Which means they might work, but they can also interact with other meds or come with side effects, Dr. Malik says. Plus, the time you waste trying different OTC options can lead to (gulp) shrinkage as erectile tissue becomes fibrotic. So, if you think you have ED, skip the supplements and see your doc, like, now.

The theory behind jelqing, which is giving yourself an extra intense hand job, is that doing so creates micro-tears. In muscle-building, at least, the healing of micro-tears can result in strength and size overall. But…

…your penis isn’t a muscle. Which means that jelqing could cause serious irreversible damage to the blood vessels in your penis and to your penis itself. The so called “technique” has no science behind it and can even cause permanent ED, Dr. Malik says. You’re better off working out your pelvic floor.

Some research does link ejaculation to certain health improvements (less stress, deeper sleep, even immune function).

A lot of guys think they need to have sex or masturbate whenever they get hard to keep their erectile tissue healthy. “You need to keep getting erections to keep your tissue healthy, and your body does that as long as you're healthy,” says Dr. Malik. If you regularly notice that you’re not hard when you wake up in the middle of the night, or you don’t have morning wood, see your doc. It may be a sign of fibrosis of the erectile tissue, which can lead to penis shrinkage.

In specialized cases, a penis pump or medical-grade vacuum erection device (VED) can help some men. Both devices create negative pressure to draw blood into the penis, which can result in an erection. For guys about to get a penile implant, a penis pump can help them “get a little bit of a larger implant,” says Dr. Malik. For men who have had a radical prostatectomy (that’s a surgery for prostate cancer that can lead to a loss of penile length), they can maintain their penile length with VED.

There's little to no data that penis pumps work to enhance length or girth for the average guy, Dr. Malik says. In fact, the European Association of Urology reviewed all the science on penile enhancement with VEDs and found scarce evidence that these devices provide any aesthetic benefit. What does: Manscaping. An overgrown bush can hide a large part of your penis, so grooming your pubic hair is easy (and way cheaper).

Testosterone levels do start to dip after age 40. And T factors into a strong libido, erectile function, and sexual satisfaction. For men who develop testosterone deficiency and experience symptoms (low desire, ED, etc.), TRT can help.

Testosterone levels fluctuate all the time—"the variability even within individuals ranges from 18 to 50 percent,” says Dr. Malik. So, if you haven’t been into sex, or can’t get it up once in a while, your T may not be the issue. First focus on eating healthier, reducing stress, and sleeping better. If the issues stick around, then see a doctor.

Honestly, there isn’t one. Your penis is fine.

Being bigger won’t necessarily make you better in bed. That’s because 85 percent of women need clitoral stimulation to orgasm, Dr. Malik says, which typically doesn’t happen through vaginal penetration alone. Because the clitoris is not located at the back of the vaginal canal (that’s the cervix, and hitting it can be painful for some women), a longer penis doesn’t mean more pleasure. A skilled tongue, faster fingers, and/or the right tools (read: a vibrator) will though.

#4836. I Play Rocky Tells Sylvester Stallone’s Underdog Story. Here’s What Really Happened.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

The new biopic revisits the actor-turned-screenwriter’s long-shot fight to get Rocky made.

ROCKY IS A work of fiction, but it’s fair to say Sylvester Stallone threw his heart and suffering onto the page. The then-29-year-old actor-turned-screenwriter was a Hollywood nobody when the boxing movie to end all boxing movies was filmed in early 1976 (with a release later that year). The now-80-year-old had done minor work in largely forgotten films (oh, and don’t forget the porno!) when he wrote himself his dream leading role and convinced studio United Artists to both make the film and take a chance on the hardscrabble, sometimes literally hard-to-understand Sly as the star.

This story is recounted in I Play Rocky, the acclaimed biopic about the making and myth behind both Rocky and Stallone, played by Anthony Ippolito. Sly is, alas, “all but indivisible” from his creation, as The Guardian wrote in a review of his new memoir The Steps, “each an extension of the other.” Sly has his own version of his ascension, though it’s laced with frustration toward family and a certain producer on Rocky who he feels fleeced him (more on that below).

But what’s real in I Play Rocky, what’s Hollywood-ified, and what’s Stallone’s own hard-won truth? Here we dig into the facts behind Rocky’s development, production, and eventual gangbusters box office reception. But we also get into Stallone’s life and career, where the two merge with Rocky “The Italian Stallion” Balboa, and how well I Play Rocky streamlines it all into popcorn fun.

Sylvester Stallone was born on July 6, 1946, in Hell’s Kitchen, then a rough neighborhood of Manhattan, according to History. As Sly tells it in a (fascinating) 1976 profile in The New York Times, he was raised by a “bickering Italian couple” who put him in foster care while they worked. (His hairdresser father, Francesco “Frank” Stallone Sr., who had a tiny part in Rocky as the timekeeper in the climax fight, is embodied by a curmudgeonly Matt Dillon in I Play Rocky. Stallone’s mother, Jacqueline “Jackie” Stallone, is not depicted, but had a wild career as an astrologer, trapeze artist, chorus girl, women’s-only gym owner, and boxing promoter.)

Stallone became a juvenile delinquent who “attended 12 schools by the time he was 15, and was kicked out of most of them.” More promisingly, the native New Yorker went to high school in Philadelphia, aka Rocky town, and threw himself into sports, being a star fullback and discus thrower. In an unexpected move, he then attended university at American College in Leysin, Switzerland, where he picked up a part-time job chasing men away from female dorms, except he found it was more lucrative to “look the other way” for two francs an hour (money that scored him flights back home).

Studying drama came next at the University of Miami for two years before he moved back to New York with the loftiest thespian ambitions. Instead, he found work as an usher at a movie theater and cleaning cages at a zoo. I Play Rocky starts with a very broke Stallone as a theater usher, though there’s no zoo action, and the story cuts the very funny fact that he was fired from said theater when he tried scalping a M*A*S*H ticket to the theater’s owner, Walter Reade. (Also absent from I Play Rocky: Among Sly’s ambitions was a fully autobiographical film that he planned to call From Roaches to Riches.)

Sly took what scraps he could in his New York days, appearing in the low-budget greaser comedy The Lords of Flatbush (contrary to I Play Rocky, he was a co-lead actor, and even wrote additional dialogue). He had an uncredited bit part in Robert Altman’s 1970 touchstone M*A*S*H (yes, the same film for which he tried to scalp a ticket) and acted in Capone (1975) as well as the Roger Corman-produced cult B-movie Death Race 2000 (1975), playing Machine Gun Joe Viterbo.

That’s not all. In desperate need of money, the real-life Italian Stallion took a part in the 1970 softcore porn film The Party at Kitty and Stud's, in which he lets it all hang out—without hardcore sex. He thought the movie was garbage, but he was paid $200 for two days of work. “It was either do that movie or rob someone because I was at the end—at the very end—of my rope,” Stallone told Playboy in 1978, according to Far Out.

California came calling. With the tiniest bit of fame to his name, he moved to Los Angeles with his first wife Sasha Czack (AnnaSophia Robb in I Play Rocky), where they lived in a one-and-a-half-bedroom apartment ''in the pancreas of Hollywood,” he told the Times, for $215 a month.

“Things weren’t going so well there,” Stallone said in an archival interview quoted by Forbes. “As a matter of fact, I actually had to go out and try to sell my dog because it was either that or he wasn’t going to be very well fed around the house.” In I Play Rocky, you see Stallone actually sell his bull mastiff Butkus—then locate and buy back Butkus, who would go on to be the dog in Rocky—though it’s hard to verify if things unfolded exactly this way.

Inspiration came when he watched the championship fight in 1975 between Chuck Wepner, a club fighter known as ''The Bayonne Bleeder,'' and world champion Muhammad Ali. “And for one brief moment, this supposed stumblebum turned out to be magnificent,” Stallone later mused, according to Forbes. “I thought if this isn’t a metaphor for life.”

The lore is that based on this brief moment, Stallone went on a tear, writing the script for Rocky in just three and a half days. This becomes a crucial montage in I Play Rocky, with Sly putting pen to paper, then snoozing while his wife types it out. In reality, Stallone told the Times that he had the fight in his mind for a month, “my inspiration stage. Then I let it incubate for 10 months, the incubation stage.” Finally, writing the screenplay in a mad dash was merely “the verification stage.” Stallone loves stages.

Much of the tension in I Play Rocky actually takes place before a frame of Rocky is shot. Stallone gets a meeting with two producers, Irwin Winkler (P.J. Byrne) and Robert Chartoff (Toby Kebbell). When he turns out not to be right for a part, on his way out of the office, he sneaks his Rocky script onto the secretary’s desk. In reality, Stallone had already sold several scripts, mostly to television, and he simply brought up the Rocky idea to the producers, who asked to see the script.

Winkler and Chartoff, playing up much of the comedic antics and sarcasm in I Play Rocky, loved Stallone’s screenplay. They just didn’t want him to play the title role. The producers were contracted with United Artists. The top brass threw out star names like Burt Reynolds, James Caan, and Ryan O’Neal. But Sly refused to sell the script unless he took the lead role. And refused again. Despite the fact that he had no car and $106 in the bank.

In I Play Rocky, the figure offered to buy the script on the condition that Stallone will not play Rocky goes up to an astronomical $360,000 (which in today’s money would be $2.1 million); however, the 1976 Times profile reports that bidding went up to $265,000. Either way, a beautiful heap of money. Finally, the producers and studio greenlit Rocky with a $1 million budget and paid Stallone $35,000 plus his acting fee. Stallone was Rocky Balboa. The entire production lasted 28 days, ''the gestation time for a water bug,'' Sly quipped to the Times.

Here’s the more important part of the contract that’s left out of I Play Rocky: Stallone sold the rights to Rocky and its characters in accepting the deal. Those rights went to Winkler—which has given Winkler a fortune plus power over the Rocky franchise, and fueled an ongoing feud between the 95-year-old producer and Stallone, who’s not shy about badmouthing Winkler. Stallone is adamant that he was swindled. Per Collider, he has called Winkler “nefarious” and “the remarkably untalented and parasitical producer of Rocky and Creed.”

Despite this supposed crooked deal, Stallone came out more than fine. What’s also not in I Play Rocky is that the then-unknown received 10 percent of the net profits (known as net points in the industry) of Rocky off the backend. Given that Rocky earned roughly $200 million at the box office, becoming the top hit of 1976—on top of picking up 10 Oscar nominations and an illustrious run in ancillary business—Stallone easily made millions off the original movie. (He claims $2.5 million, Winkler claims much higher.) He is leaps and leaps richer now.

Many forget that upon release, the critical response to Rocky was mixed, split between pans and raves. But it energized the masses, and its classic status is unquestionable now. In real life and I Play Rocky, Stallone comes out with a smile on his face, aware that his and his character’s rise from forgotten bum to underdog sensation is complete.

Are you a fan of Rocky? (If you’re not, how the hell are you reading this article?) How about Rocky II, Rocky III, the Creed movies? If so, yes, yes, yes, and again yes. On the other hand, if you don’t like Hollywood behind-the-scenes tales, boxing, or Rocky, sit this one out.

Though it fudges some turns of events and details, smoothing out the messiness and politics of a young star making his way in Hollywood, its insights can be revelatory—for example, the incredible contribution of Steadicam inventor Garrett Brown (played by real-life camera operator Michael Fuchs), whose experimental invention not only made the original Rocky possible on its shoestring budget and tight schedule, but brought a distinctive graceful movement to Rocky’s training and fighting scenes. The cast is all-around captivating; Ippolito finds soul in Stallone while managing a difficult and eccentric accent.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, as directed by Peter Farrelly (Green Book), I Play Rocky is also on the schmaltzy side. But when Sly, or Ippolito, sprints up those Philadelphia Art Museum steps determined to change history, your heart will do a little jump for him.

#4834. Rare glob-eyed fish spotted in ocean’s twilight zone

Published Oct 29, 2026 2:01 PM EDT

Few deep-sea species will cause an entire research vessel’s crew to rush into the control room to catch a glimpse—but the barreleye fish (Macropinna microstoma) is one of them. During the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute’s (MBARI) recent eight-day Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition, oceanographers aboard the David Packard were reunited with one of these rare, surreal creatures for the first time in nearly five years. This time, they successfully recorded the ethereal fish using a high-resolution 4K camera attached to Doc Ricketts, the ship’s remotely operated vehicle (ROV).

“Seeing a barreleye fish is a rare treat,” Steven Haddock, a MBARI senior scientist, said in the institute’s announcement. “Crew from across the ship joined the science team in the control room, mesmerized by this remarkable animal.”

M. microstoma swims through the ocean’s twilight zone, a dim region around 2,000 feet deep in the water column. “Swims” may be a bit generous, however. The barreleye fish spends most of its time drifting in place, while using its large fins to maintain stability. Acute vision is pointless in the near-dark water, so M. microstoma evolved a truly unique set of eyes. The tubular organs roll back far enough to gaze upwards through transparent tissue in its head to hunt for prey. Subtle shadows alert the fish to a target, at which point its eyes rotate forward so it can pursue the potential meal.

Biologists are also fascinated by M. microstoma eyes’ green lenses, which resemble those of the strawberry squid (Histioteuthis heteropsis). Researchers theorize the pigment allows the fish to spot bioluminescence, giving it an additional tool to maneuver through the murky depths.

MBARI marine biologists have conducted around 7,000 ROV dives over almost 40 years of ocean surveys. In the process, they’ve amassed more than 41,000 hours of video footage.. Researchers have only spotted 11 barreleye fish in all that time, and their most recent encounter occurred in 2021.

“[The barreleye fish] reminds us of the surprising ways that animals have adapted to thrive in the ocean’s midwater,” added Haddock. “So many of them survive by looking for subtle optical cues…pitting bioluminescent camouflage against increasingly sophisticated visual capabilities.”

YETI IS KNOWN to drop a lot of product. The Austin-based brand emerged as a key player in the cooler category and has since grown immensely, putting out everything from fleeces to outdoor furniture.

The Lowlands Blanket, an durable outdoor blanket, might be a piece that gets overlooked in the brand’s offering. The original came out a few years back but Yeti has added some new colors as well as improvements like the diamond-stitched pattern. It’s waterproof, claims to repel dirt and pet hair, and comes in a host of core and seasonal colors (not to mention two different sizes). As an all-purpose, throw-kind of blanket, it’s meant to be put to use pretty much anywhere, from the back of your car or atop some cold bleachers at the soccer game to the campsite or picnic at the beach or state park.

Do you need one though? That all depends. The $200 blanket proved quite capable during testing, packing down nicely and drying at speed. There are pros and cons to the thing, and it really depends on the lifestyle you’re trying to cater to, not to mention the elements you might be operating under.

While we were sitting on a regular-sized Lowlands Blanket during the summer months (quite literally), packing it to a few outdoor concerts and park picnics, we mostly waited patiently for fall. We wanted to really assess the burly, insulated build of the thing and its waterproofness. We spent several weeks with the blanket in the back of the car, at the ready for everything from dog naps and post-paddle warmups to hangouts near the wet soccer field or full-fledged fall camping trips.

Right out of the gate, this is easily one of the most comfortable outdoor blankets we’ve tested in recent history. Down blankets can offer a similar level of sensory joy but the softness of the topside of this blanket feels like something you’d get draped over the best chair in a ski lodge, right in front of the great room fire. It’s mildly fuzzy on one side and more coarse and rugged on the other.

The seasonal colors really pop and add some flavor while the two sizes of the blanket are actually quite distinct and useful in their own ways. The smaller, about 28-in. by 38-in., is about the size of a dog bed and is (surprise) best for pets—setting up a dry sitting spot for one, or thawing wipe downs after playing in the snow. It does not come with a carrying case but rolls up plenty small and doesn’t necessitate one. The larger (the one we tested), measuring 55-in. by 78-in., is more like a bed topper, great for picnics, topping your camp bed, or just wearing around in the cold.

The corner loops are a nice touch for securing the blanket in blustery conditions and can also be used for hanging or tying down valuables. We even tried hanging it up and utilizing it as a temporary wind barrier during outings that involved occasional sideways rain. We found that it worked well as a barrier during offseason camping trips. In other words, as a comforter of sorts to protect you from dirt or the elements while keeping your base-layers or sheets beneath dry.

Cleaning the thing is pretty simple, whether that be a quick wipe-down to address grass stains and mud or a full machine wash after a weekend camping in the woods. One of the blanket’s biggest merits is its thickness, offering more depth than most at close to a half-inch. You can genuinely feel it too. Often, when you throw a packable blanket atop the grass or the sand at the beach you’re banking on the inherent softness of that natural surface and not getting much else. Not so with the Yeti, as it does afford a true layer of added comfort, one that can easily eat up contours in uneven surfaces or small rocks and sticks.

Yeti tends to follow the go big or go home philosophy, which we’re used to at this point and oftentimes suits the product and its intentions well. At nearly six pounds, it’s admittedly a bit heavy for a blanket. But you can feel instantly where all that weight is going (the ample insulation and reinforced exterior). The weight is not a huge deal, especially if you utilize the packing bag that it comes with, which you can grab by hand or sling over your shoulder. It’s more noticeable if you’re just carrying it about unfolded or rearranging that picnic spread. But, because it translates to more comfort and durability, we’re all for it. Just keep it in mind for towing purposes if you’re looking for something to pack along on a hike, you can find something far lighter.

The internet has alerted us to the possibility of mold if not dried off properly or machine-washed fairly often. While we didn’t experience that, the blanket is thicker and seemingly takes on odors a bit more than some. What’s perhaps more of an issue is the noise, which is only relatively louder than, say, a puffy blanket, which tends to offer a more whispered kind of sound when moving about beneath it. This is probably only a real issue for sensitive sleepers.

For do-it-all blankets built for the outdoors, there are a few alternatives. Rumpl has a line of nimble options that often come in cool patterns. The price is right but you’re generally getting either a mat or a puffy (although you can certainly pair the two up for more waterproofness). They’re billed as weather-resistant and while they look great and feel like snuggling into a zipped sleeping bag, they don’t quite have the waterproof build and toughness of Yeti. However, if you’re after a high warmth-to-weight ratio, it’s tough to go wrong here. Nomadix makes another quality option, a puffer blanket that packs more tightly than most, weighs just two pounds, and is even made with a bunch of recycled material. Yet, if you’re going to be dealing with more than wet grass (e.g. snow) or plan to be in more than low-level precipitation, you’ll want something more substantial.

White Duck Outdoors makes a solid one too in the Trailside Blanket, which comes in under $100, weighs just three pounds, has a streamlined layer of insulation, and smart magnetic closures for when you want to wear it. While a lot of Pendleton’s blankets are form over function, the Oregon brand does make a nice all-weather option in the Roll-Up Blanket, priced comparably to the new Yeti. It does come armed with a weather-resistant nylon side and a soft wool side to hang out on.

For an all-purpose outdoor blanket that can take you from the snowy slopes to the trail and pretty much everywhere in between, this is a tough one to beat. It’s more durable than many we’ve tested, offers more comfort by way of added depth and nicely-stitched insulation, and even fends off pet hair swimmingly. While a great accompaniment to camping adventures, the Lowlands Blanket is also great for elevating the outdoor music festival, throwing atop a damp yard, or lugging to the tailgater (especially in the fall and winter).

This regular size is $200, a fair chunk of change (the small version is $75). And while that’s not cheap, it simply outdoes just about every other blanket in its class. You may not need a heavier, weatherproof blanket if you mostly spend time car camping. But if you want a burly blanket that’s not afraid of the terrain or weather, this one’s for you. Offseason campers are wise to consider it, as are diehard sports fans who like to show up for their team.

#4831. MIT develops robot that slithers through intestines like a snake

Published Oct 29, 2026 3:10 PM EDT

Worms are usually the last thing someone wants in their gut. Just ask this unfortunate Alaskan bear recently spotted with several multi-foot long tapeworms hanging out of its butt. However, a  new type of gut-crawling worm being designed by engineers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), may actually be here to help.

Their soft robot, called BIOSENTER, is designed to autonomously inch through the crowded, cramped, and coiled small intestine, contracting and extending its body much like an earthworm or snake. It does that by alternately pumping air through four inflatable chambers on either side of its hollow body. Once inside, the wiggly worm-bot can snap photos, administer drugs, and even take small biopsy samples. It can also slither into the intestine via a person’s mouth or rear-end all by itself.

Horrifying as all of this might sound, the team behind it says the robot could offer a faster, less labor-intensive alternative to double-balloon enteroscopy, the current standard for examining  the small intestine. And with intestinal diseases and cancers on the rise, any methods to detect issues early could have potentially life-saving results. The team published details about the robot this week in the journal Science Robotics.

The small intestine is a particularly challenging place to run diagnoses. Though it can measure 20 feet long, it’s tightly coiled up in a cramped part of the abdomen. It is also hemmed in by the stomach and colon, which can make it difficult to reach.  But bleeding, lessons, and blockages can develop in the small intestine which can lead to big problems if left untreated. Currently, the most common way to examine the organ is double-balloon enteroscopy. Healthcare workers repeatedly inflate and deflate two balloons to work a scope through the digestive tract. The method works, but it’s slow and requires constant hands-on attention.

“The fundamental challenge that we’re trying to overcome is how to evaluate that 20-to-25-foot segment of the small intestine in a way that can be more automated,” Giovanni Traverso, an MIT mechanical engineer and  study-co-author, said in a statement.

The team turned to nature for a solution: snakes. These scaly reptiles move by alternating contracting muscles on either side of their body. Aside from offering protection, their scaly bodies also give them extra traction as they slither. The MIT researchers looked at this natural byproduct of evolution and saw a design that could work well in the narrow, slippery corridors of the human GI tract.

With the snake inspiration in mind, the team built a soft, rubbery robot with a hollow body. Its worm-like frame measures about 3.7 inches in length with a half inch diameter. These dimensions make it compact enough to travel through the small intestine, as well as other narrow passages in the body, like the esophagus. BIOSENTER has four inflatable chambers arranged along either side of its tubular body.  These chambers inflate and deflate in alternating combinations, which is how it moves forewarn and bends to change directions. Keeping with the snake theme, the robot’s exterior is fitted with a textured, scale-like coating that improves its traction.

Additionally, the worm has expandable sections built in its head and tail inspired by a type of Japanese origami called kirigami, that uses cuts as well as folds. These inflatable segments alternately grip and release the intestinal wall, anchoring the robot so it can pull itself forward. BIOSENTER’s hollowed out body houses a variety of tools: cameras for imaging, a sprayer for drug delivery, and tiny clippers to take tissue samples. The entire thing is tethered to an external system via cable. Though it’s meant to move mostly autonomously, healthcare workers can also control BIOSENTER through a handheld device reminiscent of an Xbox controller.

“By using kirigami sleeves to enhance surface friction, the robot can generate localized tissue engagement traction for locomotion without relying on excessive stretching of the delicate small intestinal tissue,” added MIT graduate student Ahmad Mujtaba Jebran..

The team tested the robot on several sedated,  living pigs, because their GI tract anatomy resembles the kind humans have. During testing, BIOSENTER navigated the pigs’ intestines for 11 minutes, capturing real-time images, collecting small tissue biopsies, and delivering fluid to specific locations.

BIOSENTER notably isn’t the first gut-crawling robot. In 2021, a team from the University of Macau in China designed a prototype robot inspired by an African spider that moves using a cartwheel motion. In that case, the robot is injected via a vitamin sized capsule and traverses the GI tract (including the small intestine) via a magnetic field. Rather unglamorously, the spider bot is expelled by pooping.

#4830. Someone ran Rivian’s pedal-by-wire e-bike out of battery and things got weird

The ALSO TM-B is one of the most technologically interesting new e-bikes to hit the road in years, largely because it does away with one of the most fundamental parts of a bicycle: the mechanical connection between the pedals and rear wheel. With only copper wires connecting the pedals to the rear wheel, the TM-B is one of the most revolutionary new e-bikes in years.

But that raises an obvious question. What happens when the battery dies?

One early Launch Edition owner, Aaron Draczynski, decided to find out by deliberately running his TM-B down toward empty to see whether ALSO’s drive-by-wire system would leave him stranded.

He shared the experience on YouTube, discovering that the answer is surprisingly complicated – and involves something called “Infinite Turtle Mode.”

Unlike a conventional e-bike, where the rider’s pedaling mechanically turns the rear wheel through a chain or belt, the ALSO TM-B uses a pedal-by-wire drivetrain. Pedaling generates electricity, while the rear wheel is driven electrically.

That arrangement enables all sorts of interesting features, including electronically simulated gearing and the Launch Edition’s massive Level 10 boost mode, which can multiply rider input by up to 10 times.

But it also means there’s no traditional drivetrain to fall back on when the battery runs out.

Fortunately, the bike doesn’t simply go from full power to dead.

The owner began his experiment at 31% charge and quickly watched the bike progressively restrict its maximum assist as the battery drained closer to empty. From 23% to 13%, the maximum boost dropped from Level 8 to Level 5 as it began conserving battery.

By 10% charge, the bike was limited to Level 4. At 8%, it dropped to Level 3, followed by Level 2 at 5%. Shortly afterward, only Level 1 remained. Then at 4% battery, conventional electric assistance disappeared entirely.

Interestingly, the normal electronic shifting of the bike’s simulated software gears continued to work through most of that process. But when the battery reached 4%, things changed as the bike started exhibiting issues. The first sign of trouble came when the bike began seemingly randomly shifting gears while in manual mode without the rider even touching the shifter. Several times per second, the bike seemed to want to shift itself between gears.

Keep in mind that the TM-B doesn’t have actual physical gears (and no chain or derailleur, for that matter), but instead simulates various gears using predefined software to make the rider feel like they are working more or less intensely to pedal the bike.

Once the TM-B reached its final low-battery state, an infinity symbol appeared on the display and the bike entered what the owner referred to as “Infinite Turtle Mode.”

Instead of using stored battery energy to provide meaningful assistance, the system effectively attempts to pass the rider’s pedaling energy through the electronic drivetrain to keep the rear wheel turning. It’s similar in concept to those old crank-powered flashlights, which, even with a dead storage battery, would still illuminate for as long as the owner cranked them.

And on flat ground, the owner reported that the infinite turtle mode apparently worked surprisingly well.

Draczynski described the experience as roughly equivalent to pedaling a normal bicycle in fourth gear. There was resistance at the pedals, and he could maintain a reasonable pace without feeling like he was simply spinning his legs uselessly.

Then he reached a hill and found the limitation of that effectiveness. Even a slight incline transformed the experience, with the bike feeling more like it was permanently stuck in seventh or eighth gear. Getting home through his hilly neighborhood became, in his words, a “truly grueling ordeal.”

Manual shifting was also disabled in this mode, meaning there was no way to electronically select an easier virtual gear for climbing, since again, there aren’t any physical gears in the bike. Everything in the pedaling experience is software-simulated.

That’s an important limitation for a bike relying entirely on a drive-by-wire drivetrain. The infinite turtle mode might keep you moving with significant effort on level terrain, but it doesn’t turn a dead TM-B into a conventional bicycle, unless that conventional bicycle is being ridden through beach sand.

The low-power state apparently shuts down some other features as well. The owner could no longer lock or unlock the TM-B through ALSO’s smartphone app, though he did report the bike’s touchscreen controls continued working, and he guessed that the bike had shut down connectivity to conserve power for its key systems to operate.

Perhaps more concerning than the low-battery riding experience was what happened when this particular TM-B was simply sitting in the owner’s garage.

Describing another scenario he encountered, Draczynski says he left the bike sitting unplugged in his garage at around 70% charge. The following evening, it had fallen to 40%, and a day later it was down to 18%.

When he returned the next morning, the TM-B displayed a “Bike issue detected” message followed by “Install battery to ride.”

There was just one problem: the battery was already installed.

Plugging in the charger didn’t initially help because the bike apparently couldn’t detect its own battery, and thus charging didn’t begin. Worse, the battery refused to eject using the normal ejection process, leaving the owner unable to remove it and charge it off of the bike.

Ultimately, Draczynski used the physical reset button underneath the frame, which brought the system back to life. The bike recognized the battery again and began charging normally.

Much like modern EVs, I would imagine a lot of these issues will be fixed via a software update. Early adoption is fun but you’re basically beta testing a product for the company at full price.

That degree of overnight battery drain obviously isn’t something we’d expect from a normal e-bike, so hopefully this was either an isolated software issue or something ALSO can address with an update. For his part, Draczynski suspects that the bike might be draining its battery so heavily at rest due to the lack of a cell signal in his garage. “I was quite surprised at the drop from day to day,” he explained on Reddit. “If I had to wager a guess, the bike might be searching for a cellular signal, but there’s no reception in my garage so it’s just draining the battery.”

But the experiment offers an interesting first real-world look at one of the biggest questions surrounding ALSO’s unusual drivetrain.

A normal e-bike with a dead battery becomes a heavy bicycle. The TM-B instead becomes something much stranger: an electricity-generating exercise machine that uses your legs to generate current, electronically sends that current through the bike, and then uses it to turn the rear wheel.

And based on this testing, it does in fact work. Just try not to be at the bottom of a hill when you find out for yourself.
