#4794. Josh O’Connor Should Be James Bond

The Challengers star would bring a new energy—and a new brand of modern masculinity—to the world’s most famous spy.

WHEN THE NAMES of the rumored final contenders to play the next James Bond were floated in the press a couple of weeks ago—seemingly Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, and a mystery third candidate, according to Deadline—I heard a lot of the same sentiment afterward. In more or less words, a lot of people seemed to say “I love Josh O’Connor, but he shouldn’t be Bond.” When I dropped the link into a group chat full of people who aren’t inhaling movie news like I am, there was another probably common response: “I don’t know who that guy is, but he doesn’t look like Bond.”

To me, that sentiment is exactly why O’Connor is the best—and, in some ways, the only—choice to be the next James Bond.

For those not familiar, O’Connor, a 36-year-old Brit who grew up in Cheltenham, has been a working actor for more than a decade, but his star has only really begun to shine in the 2020s. He won an Emmy for playing Prince Charles in The Crown, and more recently has made splashes in movies like the thrilling and sexy sports film Challengers, Rian Johnson’s third Knives Out film Wake Up Dead Man (which, ironically, he appeared in alongside previous Bond Daniel Craig), and this summer’s Steven Spielberg blockbuster Disclosure Day.

It’s not hard to understand why some people’s minds might naturally push against the idea of O’Connor as Bond. Where 007 is typically a classically handsome, devilishly smooth gentleman who almost looks like a video game simulation—seriously, look back at Sean Connery and Pierce Brosnan for just a second—O’Connor is a bit off-kilter. His hair is wavy; his ears are prominent; his smile is asymmetrical. There’s no beating around the bush—he’s been compared more often to Linguini from Pixar’s Ratatouille than the idea most people have of what a James Bond should be.

But it’s through those eccentricities that O’Connor shines. If you take the time to watch his performances, you’ll find the constant image of someone who brings an undeniable charisma to every project, and somehow manages to mold that into something different each time. In Challengers, O’Connor is the kind of guy you want to root against—he’s sleazy, not a particularly good friend, and unrefined. But he brings the perfect bit of steamy, compelling energy to a love triangle that wouldn’t be the same without him. Co-stars Mike Faist and Zendaya are deserving of credit (as are composers Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross), but O’Connor’s charm is what makes the whole movie work.

He pulls a similar magic trick with just about every other performance. In Wake Up Dead Man, he plays a former boxer-turned-priest who once accidentally killed a man in the ring. Throughout the course of the film, O’Connor goes from someone who wrestles with guilt, shame, and intrigue to someone who can believably talk someone struggling with grief off a ledge—all while both trying to solve a murder and possibly being suspected of that same murder at the same time. In Kelly Reichardt’s The Mastermind, O’Connor plays a less-than-competent, hardly aspirational art thief who stumbles his way through charged political times. Despite this, O’Connor is so magnetic on screen that it’s just about impossible not to like him.

But it’s not just the way he elevates sleazeballs and losers into undeniably watchable men (although that doesn’t hurt). O’Connor has shown a propensity to play traditionally enchanting as well. In La Chimera, from Italian filmmaker Alice Rohrwacher, he’s cool, sleek, and morally gray in a movie that may be the blueprint for what his Bond could potentially look like. He’s got a likable way about him that’s different from some of the manly men (like Connery), sleek operators (like Brosnan), or rugged action stars (like Craig) who’ve played the role before; His charm is distinctly more modern, oozing from nothing other than being a guy who knows how to talk to people, and do it really well.

O’Connor’s quirks and oddities, may, at first glance, be what seems to make him an unfit choice to play Bond. But the key is to look at O’Connor’s unique look and gifts as a feature rather than a bug. People might say Bond needs to look this way, and sound that way, and otherwise it doesn’t work. But for anyone who feels so strongly about that, there’s good news: There are 25 other canonical James Bond movies (plus 1967’s Casino Royale and 1983’s Never Say Never Again) where he almost always looks and behaves just like that. When better than now to try something new? Daniel Craig’s blond hair and untraditional look were also questioned at first, and it’s safe to say that risk turned out pretty well in the end.

The forthcoming Bond movie has Denis Villeneuve signed on as director, and Villeneuve has pretty much never failed when it comes to casting his movies. Can you imagine anyone other than Timothée Chalamet as Paul Atreides in his Dune movies? It seems like an obvious pick now, but the 30-year-old Oscar nominee had only just begun to break out when he was cast in the role back in 2018. Villeneuve has a clear eye for talent, and so it won’t be much of a stretch to trust in whoever ultimately lands the job—but it’s hard to not be excited about a director of his caliber linking up with an actor as ambitious and high-reaching as O’Connor.

Plus, it’s worth noting that the Bond franchise isn’t quite like other mega-series out there. Since the Craig era began with 2006’s Casino Royale, Bond movies have come out on average every three or four years. That’s spread out enough for O’Connor to continue taking on fun, exciting projects even outside of the role as everyone’s favorite super spy.

The other choices aren’t bad. Callum Turner gets a bad rap after his appearance in One Night Only, but he’s shown promise in projects like Green Room and Masters of the Air, and Apple TV’s new Neuromancer looks good. Jack Lowden has played one of television’s most beloved spies for six seasons on Slow Horses—the fit would be seamless. Whoever Villeneuve picks (even if it’s the unnamed mystery actor) will be afforded a huge amount of goodwill.

But isn’t the fact that O’Connor elicits such a reaction—consistently in his on-screen roles and through the mere idea of him becoming James Bond—proof that he’s the right pick?

#4793. Tesla drops car referral rewards, now pays owners in FSD for referrals

Tesla has launched a new referral program in the US that pays owners in Full Self-Driving (Supervised) instead of rewarding car sales. A referred owner gets one free month of FSD, and the referrer gets a free month or a $99 Tesla Credit if that person starts paying.

At the same time, Tesla’s Refer and Earn terms no longer list any vehicle as a qualifying purchase for buyer or referrer rewards. Buy a Tesla with a friend’s code today and neither of you gets anything.

To share a link, you need to be paying for FSD (Supervised) monthly or own it outright from before Tesla stopped selling it, according to Tesla’s FSD referral support page. Owners who got FSD through a one-year grant can’t participate. The link lives under “Refer and Earn” in the Tesla app, version 4.62.0 or later.

The person on the other end has to own a registered Tesla with compatible hardware, can’t have paid for FSD in the past 12 months, and can’t have bought it outright. There’s also a catch for recent buyers: anyone who got a free FSD trial with a new car is locked out of referral links until 12 months after that trial ends.

The bigger change is buried in Tesla’s Refer and Earn page. Buyer benefits now apply to solar panels only. Referrer benefits cover solar, first demo drives (up to 30 over an account’s lifetime) and the new FSD referral.

Model 3, Model Y and Cybertruck only show up under loyalty benefits, for existing owners buying another Tesla product. Model S and Model X aren’t listed at all.

Tesla didn’t announce the change. The page is stamped “Updated February 24, 2026,” so it’s unclear exactly when vehicles came off the list.

That’s quite a turn for a program that was always about moving cars. When Tesla brought the referral program back in August 2024, a buyer got $1,000 off a Model S, X, Y or 3, and the referrer got $500 in credit. Tesla has killed and revived the program several times over the past decade, but cars were always at the center of it. Not anymore.

That’s the exact metric in Elon Musk’s 2025 CEO Performance Award, which includes a milestone of 10 million active FSD subscriptions. It’s the reason Tesla started disclosing the number in January in the first place.

The free month a friend receives doesn’t count toward that total. A paid conversion does, and that’s precisely the event the new program pays for.

The only way I would ever pay for FSD is if Tesla covered full comprehensive insurance for my vehicle and accepted all liability. Otherwise, it's a gamble with my (and others') life.

That they seem to prioritize this sham service (Just call it Assisted Driving for honesty sake?) versus improving the cars or lowering prices, tells me enough not to look at Tesla for my next vehicle.

The recipient has to already own a Tesla, so the program doesn’t add a single car to the fleet. It’s built to mine the existing fleet for subscriptions. Tesla had sold about 8.9 million vehicles by the end of 2025, and only 1.74 million are paying for FSD, so there’s plenty of room. At Q3’s pace, we estimated 10 million subscriptions is still about eight years away.

So Tesla stopped paying for referrals that require selling a car, and started paying for the ones that move the number in Musk’s pay package. We think that tells you a lot about where the company’s priorities are right now.

#4792. The 8 Best Sweater Polos for Men, According to Style Editors

Your next best-dressed moment starts from the collar down.

I CONSIDER MYSELF the king of sweaters. I love a good collared shirt, so polos are my go-to in the spring and summer. But once fall and winter roll around, I’m all about sweaters. Even better: a sweater polo. It’s the perfect mashup that combines the collar and button placket of a classic polo with the knit construction of a sweater, giving you a little more texture and warmth than your standard cotton pique. The best sweater polos offer that same versatility. You can dress things up or lean super casual depending on the day and occasion. And not all have to be long-sleeved either.

Short-sleeve versions are also great for tropical vacations or layers under a blazer for the office. Either way, they’re an easy way to switch up your usual sweater rotation from the same ol’ crews or turtlenecks. The Men’s Health fashion crew and I have tried more than 30 over the last three years, paying close attention to fit, fabric, comfort, and versatility to find ones that deserve a spot in your closet.

For the past five years, I’ve tested more than 25 sweater polos, but Uniqlo is easily one of my favorites. It checks all the boxes when it comes to excellent quality, fit, versatility and what really seals the deal—affordability. At just $50, you’re getting a premium knit that could pass for something more expensive. It’s made from a cotton-blend yarn in a structured Milano rib knit that looks and feels more like woven cloth than a stretchy tee. This one feels dense yet comfortable on the skin. I especially love the buttonless, open V-neck collar, which gives some breathing room and makes the whole thing feel a little relaxed.

In terms of fit, it’s roomy through the chest and flexible through the arms without looking oversized. I’ve worn it with jeans and dressed it up with tailored trousers and loafers for dinner. Just be sure to toss it in a mesh laundry bag to keep the knit in good shape.

Yes, even in the summertime when the temps stayed around 80 degrees, I didn’t break a sweat at the backyard party. The polyester fabric feels soft against the skin and has a little stretch, which makes it easy to move around in.

It also has a V-neck polo collar to give it that laid-back vibe, while the ribbed cuffs and hem pull everything in for a more fitted, body-contouring look. Styling-wise, you’ve got plenty of options. I’d wear it untucked with jeans or chinos for an everyday fit, but you can also tuck it in pants with a belt for a day on the golf course. This one is not machine washable, so I’d recommend taking a trip to the dry cleaners.

I love mixing different textures in my polo sweater collection, so things don’t start looking too plain. That’s when I add in pieces like Charles Tyrwhitt’s textured knit to give some depth and dimension to my outfit without going overboard with loud patterns or prints. It’s made from 100 percent cotton that’s been garment-washed for a softer, broken-in feel, so I’m not dealing with a stiff, scratchy sweater.

The midweight material is substantial enough to wear on its own during cooler days but breathable enough to layer under a jacket without feeling too bundled up. I’d wear the petrol-blue shade with cream trousers and brown suede loafers for a sharp office look, or pair it with dark denim and boots for dinner. I’ve washed it more than four times and haven’t seen it shrink or pill, but my advice is to let it air dry.

When my brain can’t function in the morning to put an outfit together, I just rely on Abercrombie’s knit. It’s made from 100 percent merino wool, which sounds like it might be a recipe for itchiness, but surprisingly, it feels soft and smooth against the skin. I also dig the classic three-button collar, which gives it a slightly dressier edge than your average crewneck. The fit is also a nice balance, with enough room in the chest and stomach, in case I wolfed down a burger.

Now, I will say that the wool can get a little toasty, especially if you’re moving around a lot. But if your office blasts AC like it’s the middle of Antarctica, you should be just fine. Styling-wise, I’d wear it with straight-leg jeans and sneakers for a casual Friday, or swap in chinos and loafers when I want to look a little more put-together. It only comes in neutrals, which should be easy to pair with anything in your wardrobe.

There’s something about cashmere that makes even the simplest outfit feel a little more luxurious. And if you’re going to invest in a cashmere sweater polo, Quince is a great place to start. This one is made from 100 percent Grade-A Mongolian cashmere, with fine fibers that give the knit an incredibly soft, smooth feel. The 12-gauge construction gives it a refined look without making it feel overly chunky, and the ribbed cuffs and hem help keep its shape. And when I don’t want to wear a dress shirt, this is a great alternative. Throw it on with tailored trousers and loafers for the office, or pair it with dark jeans and boots for dinner.

I’m a big fan of merino wool because it gives you the warmth of a sweater minus all the extra bulk. Banana Republic uses it for this polo, which is a solid option that can transition from the office straight to dinner. No matter how toasty a room gets, I’m never sweating in it. The fabric stays lightweight and breathable, and has enough warmth to come in handy when temperatures drop.

I also like that the fit is pretty straightforward, with slightly dropped shoulders and ribbed cuffs and hem that give it a relaxed but clean finish. The buttoned collar makes it feel a little dressier than your average knit, especially when paired with chinos or tailored trousers. And unlike some wool sweaters that require a trip to the dry cleaner, this one is machine washable, which is always a plus in my book.

Cos gave the classic sweater polo a completely different spin with a buttonless collar that sits closed rather than opening into the usual V-neck. It’s a subtle detail, but one that makes people take a second look at my outfit. This neckline creates a cleaner, more sophisticated look without being overly flashy. I’d pair it with wide-leg trousers and leather loafers for a sharp office fit, or throw it on with relaxed jeans and sneakers for the weekend.

I especially like this kind of silhouette for guys who prefer a minimalist wardrobe but still want something with a little personality. Now, at around $130, it’s definitely on the pricier side, especially when you can find sweater polos for half that amount. But I’d argue you’re paying for a design that’s a refreshing departure from the sweater polos you’re used to seeing, and chances are, you won’t spot five other guys wearing the same thing.

Not every sweater polo needs long sleeves, especially when you can rock one under a blazer. Take this retro-inspired short-sleeve style from Bonobos, which I can wear year-round. It’s dressy enough to skip the traditional button-down shirt, whether you’re heading to an important meeting or a cocktail reception.

It’s also a great piece to pack for vacation, especially if you’re traveling somewhere tropical and need something sharp for a resort dinner. In that case, ditch the blazer and pair it with linen pants or even shorts for a more laid-back look. Plus, the breathable cotton fabric won’t make scorching temps feel even more unbearable. I wore it on a recent trip to Cancún and didn’t break much of a sweat. Depending on your personal style, Bonobos offers this sweater polo in a variety of colors, prints, and textures, so there’s plenty to choose from.

#4791. Psychedelic nasal spray treats depression with toad-inspired goo

Published Oct 30, 2026 3:45 PM EDT

A powerful psychedelic compound best associated with the Sonoran desert toad (Incilius alvarius) has been recreated in a lab and transformed into a fast-acting nasal spray. A recent clinical trial outlined this week in the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) suggests this spray could help people with treatment resistant depression, without the often less pleasant element of psychedelics. In the study, a single squeeze of the spray eased patients’ depressive symptoms with benefits lasting throughout the eight week trial.

Crucially, those long-term benefits (which have also been observed in other psychedelic research) didn’t require enduring an all-day mystical trip. Most patients were cleared for release less than two hours after taking the spray. Thankfully, the approach also eliminates the need to fondle a toxic amphibian. That’s potentially a plus both for patients and overharvested toad populations. The finds come amid a resurgence in new research and investment involving psychedelics, supported in part by evolving political attitudes towards the compounds on federal and state levels.

The nasal spray was developed by biotech firm AtaiBeckley. Its  active ingredient is called mebufotenin, which is also known as 5-MeO-DMT. The compound occurs naturally in several places, but it is most famously associated with the secretions of the Sonoran desert toad. For decades, amateur psychonauts have sought out these meaty North American toads for the prominent glands located on the amphibian’s head and hind legs. Squeezing those glands releases a milky secretion (sometimes inaccuracy referred to as venom), which when dried and then vaporized, produces an intense psychedelic experience. Many people who have smoked it describe a profound sense of oneness or ego dissolution, and some even report the sensation of dying.

Though based on the same compound, the drug in the nasal spray is synthetic and made in a lab. The researchers wanted to see if a controlled, clinical dose of 5-MeO-DMT could deliver some of the compound’s reported therapeutic benefits while keeping the overall treatment brief, especially compared with longer-acting psychedelics like psilocybin. They  limited their study to 193 adults between the ages of 18 to 75 with treatment-resistant depression. The participants, who came from the United States, Europe, and Australia, had each already tried at least two antidepressant treatments without success. By some estimates, around a third of all patients experiencing major depressive disorder also have treatment resistant depression.

Each participant received nasal spray in either a low (.3mg), medium (8mg), or high (12mg) dose. Neither the patient, nor the clinical staff or researchers involved knew which dose was given. The most intense psychedelic effects wore off relatively quickly, regardless of the dose. Clinicians checked on the patients at regular intervals to determine if they were deemed safe enough to leave the clinic. Among participants who received the 8-milligram dose, 85 percent were ready for discharge within two hours, compared with 78 percent of those who received the 12-milligram dose.

However, the therapeutic effects of the spray appeared to persist far longer.  Patients who received the medium or high dose showed significantly greater improvement than the comparison group as early as two days after treatment, and that advantage held through the end of the eight-week study. The team measured depression with a clinical scale measuring from 0 to 60, with  higher scores indicating more severe symptoms. After four weeks, the 12 mg group had dropped an average of 11.1 points on that score. The 8mg group dropped an even higher 12.5 points while the .3mg group dropped 5.5 points. These findings suggest the nasal spray application could provide some of the same therapeutic effects of other scheduled therapies less less need to have healthcare workers monitoring patients for many hours at a time.

“In adults with treatment-resistant depression, single doses of intranasal mebufotenin benzoate were well tolerated and produced rapid, robust, and durable reductions in depressive symptoms,” the study authors write. “Intranasal mebufotenin benzoate may improve treatment access and convenience, requiring a shorter monitoring period and fewer clinic visits compared with psilocybin and esketamine, respectively.”

This experimental nasal spray arrives amid a transitionary period for psychedelic research. State governments have shown more interest in the field in recent years, with Oregon and Colorado each launching their own psilocybin programs. Even Texas, a state traditionally associated with a tough on drugs approach, just committed $50 million to research the powerful psychedelic ibogaine. Signs of movement are occurring at the federal level as well. In April, President Donald Trump signed an executive order aimed at accelerating research and FDA approval of psychedelic-based therapies.

Though it attracted significant attention, the executive order is really more signaling than action. It notably does not lower the bar a therapeutic needs to reach before archived FDA approval.

Still, pharmaceutical companies are clearly taking note. Earlier this year, Eli Lilly, the largest pharmaceutical company in the world, acquired AtariBeckley for $2.8 billion. AtaiBeckley developed the nasal spray used in the recent JAMA study.

#4790. When Infants Cry Excessively, Supporting Parents Matters Too

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

If you've ever found yourself pacing the house at midnight with a crying baby in your arms, you've probably searched for one answer: How do I make the crying stop?

Much research and clinical advice has focused on that exact question. Scientists have tested probiotics, feeding approaches, soothing techniques, and other interventions designed to reduce infant crying. But there is another important question that often receives less attention: What happens to parents during this experience?

In a recent systematic review (Bilgin et al., 2026), my colleagues and I examined whether interventions used for excessive infant crying also improve outcomes for parents. Rather than focusing solely on whether babies cry less, we asked whether these interventions help parents feel less stressed, less anxious, and better able to cope.

The answer matters because excessive infant crying is not just challenging for babies. It can be profoundly difficult for parents as well.

The first months after birth are already a time of enormous adjustment. Parents are often coping with sleep deprivation, physical recovery, changes in identity, and new responsibilities. When a baby cries frequently and is difficult to soothe, these challenges can become even more intense.

Parents of excessively crying infants often report feeling overwhelmed, helpless, frustrated, and worried that something may be wrong with their baby. Many also worry that they are somehow failing as parents.

Yet excessive crying is common. Crying typically peaks during the first few months of life (Wolke, Bilgin, & Samara, 2017) and, for many infants, occurs despite sensitive and responsive caregiving. Unfortunately, parents do not always receive reassurance about this reality.

Our review brought together evidence from 29 studies involving more than 2,500 families. The studies evaluated a range of interventions, including parent-focused educational programmes and infant-focused approaches such as probiotics.

What interested us most was whether these interventions improved parental wellbeing.

We found that interventions designed to educate and support parents were particularly beneficial. Parents who received information and support reported lower levels of stress and anxiety than those who did not.

These programmes typically provided reassurance about normal infant development, information about crying patterns, practical coping strategies, and guidance on managing parental stress. In other words, they did more than address crying; they addressed the parental experience of crying.

At first glance, it may seem surprising that education could make such a difference.

But information can change how parents interpret their baby's behaviour. Without reassurance, persistent crying can easily be interpreted as a sign that something is seriously wrong or that a parent is doing something incorrectly.

When parents understand that crying often peaks in early infancy and that excessive crying is not necessarily a sign of poor parenting, the experience can become more manageable. The crying itself may not disappear immediately, but parents often feel better equipped to cope with it.

This highlights an important distinction: Reducing crying is not the only meaningful outcome. Helping parents feel less distressed is valuable in its own right.

One of the strongest messages emerging from our review is that parent wellbeing should not be treated as a secondary outcome.

When healthcare professionals meet families struggling with excessive infant crying, the focus naturally falls on the baby. Yet parents themselves may require support, reassurance, and practical guidance. Interventions that acknowledge parental experiences can help reduce feelings of isolation and self-blame while improving confidence and coping.

Parents frequently seek help because they want the crying to stop. But "How can I get through this difficult period?" may be an equally important question.

Our findings suggest that interventions providing reassurance, practical guidance, and support for parents' emotional wellbeing can help answer that question, reducing stress and anxiety while improving coping. Perhaps the most important message for parents is this: A crying baby does not mean you are doing anything wrong, and you do not have to get through it alone.

Bilgin, A., Betteridge, A., Brown, J., Boyle, E. M., Brugha, T., Fusco, F., Stracke, M., Swift, S. L., Wolke, D., & St James-Roberts, I. (2026). Interventions to Support Parents Whose Babies Cry Excessively: Systematic Review. Pediatrics; e2025075063. 10.1542/peds.2025-075063

Wolke D., Bilgin A., & Samara M. (2017). Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis: Fussing and Crying Durations and Prevalence of Colic in Infants. J Pediatr;185:55-61.e4.

THEY’VE BEEN CROPPING up everywhere. All over my social media feed, featured across men’s runway collections at Fashion Week, seen on Hollywood heartthrobs like Michael B. Jordan, and so forth. If you haven’t figured it out by now, I’m talking about the henley. This once-overlooked wardrobe staple has found new popularity, showing no signs of slowing down as it becomes one of fall’s most surprising menswear trends. And quite frankly, I’m here for it.

The henley hasn’t traditionally been the sexiest shirt in a guy’s wardrobe. For years, it’s been the tee you’d throw on for a lazy Sunday or wear underneath a flannel. But somewhere along the way, the fashion crowd decided it deserved another shot. Its roots go all the way back to 19th-century England, where it started as an undergarment before becoming a go-to for rowers in Henley-on-Thames, hence the name. Who would’ve thought a shirt with such humble beginnings would eventually become a fashion obsession on my Instagram timeline?

Cos Slim Ribbed Cotton Long-Sleeved Henley T-Shirt

Todd Snyder Lightweight Mini Waffle Henley

Cherry Los Angeles Waffle-Knit Cotton-Blend Henley T-Shirt

California Arts Murray Slim Long Sleeve Henley

Here’s what I love about the henley: It does more heavy lifting than your average T-shirt without trying to be anything fancy. You get the simplicity of a crewneck, the button placket of a polo, and just enough texture to make an otherwise basic outfit feel put-together. And while the classic cotton version is still very much in rotation, ribbed, waffle-knit, and thermal styles are giving guys even more ways to wear it. If you need further proof that the henley is having a moment, just take a peek at the runways. For Fall/Winter 2026, Paul Smith sent a model down the runway in a white henley tucked into wide-leg black trousers, while Isabel Marant took a more layered approach, pairing a light blue henley with a navy corduroy jacket.

I’m a firm believer that proportions can make or break an outfit, and the henley is no exception. My favorite way to wear one is with baggy jeans or relaxed trousers. The contrast between a fitted top and roomier bottoms creates a flattering silhouette. And if you’ve spent the past few months putting in work at the gym, a henley is one of the easiest ways to show off those gains without looking like you’re showing off. The closer fit naturally accentuates your chest, shoulders, and biceps, especially when you leave the top button or two undone. Just remember, there’s a fine line between fitted and too tight.

Whether you’re dressing one up with trousers and loafers or keeping things casual with loose jeans and boots, the henley proves that sometimes the most unexpected trends are the pieces we’ve had in our closets all along. And it’s about time this one received its flowers.

BYD is moving upmarket with its new flagship EV, featuring suicide doors, a gemstone grille, and possibly solid-state batteries.

Yangwang is like BMW’s Rolls-Royce and Mercedes-Maybach, sitting at the very top of BYD’s brand hierarchy.

The ultra-luxury brand offers BYD’s most high-end and technically advanced vehicles, including the U7 sedan, the U8, a hardcore off-road SUV, and the U9, an electric supercar.

Yangwang vehicles have previously debuted with BYD’s latest breakthrough tech, including its quad-motor e4 platform (delivering over 1,300 hp), its second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging, and its DiSus-X intelligent body control system.

Its next model will push further into the elite segment. After BYD revealed the name of its new flagship executive sedan earlier this week, the Yangwang Altior, the company has released several new details ahead of its official debut.

Yangwang general manager Hu Xiaoqing confirmed on Friday that the new Yangwang Altior will feature suicide doors, a first for a BYD model.

The new door design swings open nearly 90 degrees, Hu said, creating a dramatic, wide-open entrance.

Hu also posted a preview of the vehicle’s front fascia, complete with a dot-matrix Gemstrone grille and crystal-inspired headlights.

BYD has not confirmed many details, but the ultra-luxury sedan is expected to be about 5,500 mm (216″) in length.

Images of the disguised vehicle released last month show a similar shape and size to the Mercedes-Benz Maybach S-Class or Rolls-Royce Phantom.

The Yangwang Altrio will feature “unprecedented disruptive technology,” Zheng Yu, Yangwang’s executive general manager, said.

Yangwang’s current electric sedan, the U7, starts at 658,000 yuan ($98,000). The extended U8L, on the other hand, is the brand’s highest-priced mass-produced vehicle, starting at 1.45 million yuan ($217,000).

#4785. I Have a New Hobby. It’s Kicking My Ass.

The fastest-growing racquet sport in America may also be the cardio workout I’ve been avoiding.

This column first appeared in the Men’s Health email newsletter. The Optimized Man is a biweekly series from our editorial director as he tries out the latest, greatest, and weirdest health and wellness innovations so you don’t have to. Sign up here to get the next one.

I’VE TRIED TO build a life free of shoulds. I’m fine with woulds and coulds and their vague promise of actionability, but when you get into shoulds, you get hung up on stuff like guilt and doubt and all kinds of second-guessing. I really should work out. I really shouldn’t eat that. You think I should try and sleep more? Thanks, man. Good tip.

Shoulds, put plainly, are a problem, and this year I’ve been staring down two different shoulds that won’t quit staring back: I should probably do more cardio, and I should probably get a hobby. I’ve never been much of a cardio guy or a hobby guy, but with evidence tying both to better physical and mental health outcomes, my list of excuses for not doing either is growing short. And I think I’ve found a solution in one of the fastest-growing sports in America.

It’s called padel (pronounced pa-DEL), and you might’ve come across it if you’ve been on vacation lately in Central America or southern Europe (or somewhere really exotic, like Miami). I discovered it last year on a cold winter’s night, and after playing for two hours on an indoor court and emerging sweaty, sore, and exuberant, I can report that it combines everything I like about tennis, racquetball, and squash into one hard-hitting, heavy-breathing sport.

You can go ahead and YouTube the basics, and here’s the gist: You’re playing on a court that’s about three-quarters the area of a tennis court, with high glass walls along the back, some wire fencing on the sides, and a net down the middle. Instead of pickleball’s slow and endless dinking, a padel ball whirs fast off your midsize racquet (also larger and heavier than pickleball’s), and the action requires you to move. Even though it’s a doubles sport (which typically requires less movement than singles, ‘cause there’s two of you), you’re constantly chasing the ball like it’s that little golden bug in quidditch. Sprint, stop, swing, pivot, repeat. (You can also hit the ball against the back wall to launch it in reverse, back over the net, which requires a massive swing.) The first time I played, I showed up wearing sweatpants and a puffer vest over a T-shirt. Within minutes of starting I had sweat through my T-shirt, and by the end of the first set, I had sweat through the seat of my sweatpants. I looked like John Candy in Splash, post-racquetball. What can I say? I’m not a cardio guy.

And there is a lot of cardio here. Back in 2024 we noticed that tennis had started billing itself as “the world’s healthiest sport,” and we asked writer Nick Pachelli to dig into the branding to see how much of it is hype. According to Nick:

Padel isn’t tennis and tennis isn’t padel, but I’ve been playing tennis for almost four decades, and I’ve never had my ass kicked quite as hard as when I played padel.

Then there is the social aspect of it—you’re part of a pair playing another pair, and whether you’re close friends or total strangers with your partner or opponents, at least you’re not bowling alone. Nick found that when longevity researchers study tennis…

Aerobic exercise, social connection and community, some light competition, and a lot of laughs: Could padel be my new hobby? Could it be my main source of cardio? Winter’s coming and the indoor courts are calling, and with visions of John Candy huffing and puffing in my head, I should probably start training.

Richard Dorment is the editorial director of Men’s Health and Women’s Health.

#4784. The In-Between: Covert Consciousness

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

Is it possible for someone to appear to be in a deep coma, paralyzed, yet have a brain that is silently aware of all that’s going on around them?

Yes. This condition is called “locked-in syndrome,” which is an extreme example of the dichotomy of having a totally paralyzed body (except for the eyes), but an awake, perfectly conscious brain and mind.

But there are other, perhaps less well-known, medical conditions that result in a state of “semi-consciousness;” states that result from a variety of brain injuries, like stroke or head trauma, that persist sometimes for many weeks, even years.

These are called the Vegetative State (or, more correctly now, the Unresponsive Wakefulness Syndrome-UWS) and The Minimally Conscious State-MCS.

Before discussing these fascinating neurological states, to address the question, “What is consciousness?”: I believe it depends on who is offering its meaning. Neurologists, like me, will describe it as a state of being aware of one’s environment, including one’s inner environment of the “self.” Philosophers will have a different definition: consciousness is what it feels like from the inside, what constitutes “intentionality,” how we engage with the world.

In my Neurological ICU, we assess “consciousness,” or “awareness,” by asking our patients to follow commands: Give me a thumbs up. Open your eyes. Our nurses ask this every hour on the hour, as part of their around-the-clock neurological examination. The ability to follow commands will often be our first indication that someone is coming out of a coma, our first glimpse of recovery.

But if our patient cannot follow commands at the bedside, this doesn’t necessarily mean they are unaware, or unconscious. “Cognitive Motor Dissociation” is a state of disordered consciousness in which a person will not demonstrate brain activity by following commands at the bedside but is able to do so covertly. For example, a person who cannot visibly respond to commands will be able to perform a requested mental task, such as imagining lifting a finger, or playing tennis, when they are receiving specialized neurotechnology such as task-based electroencephalograms (EEGs) or functional MRI scans.

Patients who have been treated as unarousable or comatose are shown to actually “be there” by these specialized tests. Unfortunately, most of this technology is still primarily reserved for research studies at academic medical centers and is not readily available at the bedside.

So, it’s frightening to think that a patient in an apparent unconscious state has been aware all along: when their arm is caught under them while being turned, while people are speaking about their prognosis at their bedside, and they can’t object or ask questions—when they are unable to cry out or grimace or express what’s going on in their head.

After severe brain injury or illness, people don’t usually stay in a coma (from the Greek “koma,” deep sleep) very long; generally two to four weeks. If they survive, they progress to one of the “in-between” states of Unresponsive Wakefulness State or Minimally Conscious State, and then, hopefully, wake up. Some never wake up. People in the UWS retain the vegetative functions of the body, like digestion, cardiac and respiratory function, so they don’t necessarily need to be on a ventilator, and they have normal sleep-wake cycles. People in the MCS are moving closer to consciousness, although their awareness and interactions with us and their environment are inconsistent… reflecting isolated areas of cortical connectivity. Full consciousness, on the other hand, requires sustained integration of cortical nerve cell activity throughout the brain.

These in-between states can be difficult to distinguish from the “locked-in syndrome,” in which patients are paralyzed, but preserve the ability to move the eyes and to blink. Patients can look up and down and can blink to command. So, they consistently and correctly answer questions by these movements. Locked-in syndrome can occur from tumors, strokes or demyelinating diseases that knock out the ventral pons in the brainstem. The cortex above remains intact. Patients are quadriplegic, their face is paralyzed, they often cannot breathe on their own, and they can lose the all-important brainstem reflexes that permit us to cough and swallow.

Yet these patients are fully conscious. The French journalist Jean-Dominique Bauby, who at 43, suffered a pontine stroke that left him alert, but locked-in, wrote his memoir The Diving Bell and the Butterfly by painstakingly dictating one letter at a time using only his left eyelid and a code written down by his partner at his bedside. The book took about 200,000 blinks to write. Remarkable. Bauby died of pneumonia in 1997, just two days after the book was published in France.

Today, we can offer locked-in patients a way to communicate their invisible thoughts with brain-computer interface systems that allow them to select a letter through a detectable brain signal via scalp EEG or implanted cortical electrodes.

What these remarkable patients have taught me is to never assume unconsciousness. Instead, assume the best: that the person in front of me in the ICU is invisibly conscious and aware of all we are saying. They can hear what their families and their visiting friends are saying to them. And I tell each patient on rounds every day what the day will hold, how they’re doing, what we plan next.

If I am wrong, and they are completely unconscious, no harm done. If I am right, whether proven by a task-based EEG or functional MRI scan, or better yet, by their waking up one day, those days and weeks have not been spent in stillness and stupor.

Tarvez Tucker, M.D., is Professor of Neurology and Neurocritical Care and a Neuroscience Intensive Care physician at Oregon Health & Science University in Portland, Oregon. She is the author of The Brain at Twilight: The Neuroscience of Our Last Words and Moments.

#4782. How This Busy Dad Got Leaner and Stronger in 11 Weeks Without Losing Much Weight

Strength coach Gareth Sapstead shares how he helped a busy dad and business owner get leaner, build muscle, and reshape his physique.

Body recomposition is widely viewed as the holy grail of physical transformation: losing body fat while simultaneously adding lean muscle.

It’s also often dismissed as either impossible or reserved exclusively for complete beginners. The logic appears fairly convincing. To lose fat, you need to consume fewer calories than you burn. To build muscle, you need enough energy to construct new tissue. One requires a deficit, the other seemingly demands a surplus.

Pick a lane: bulk first, cut later. Right?

Strength and physique coach Gareth Sapstead disagrees. In a detailed breakdown published on his website, Sapstead explains how he helped father and business owner Mark Schadenberg transform his physique ahead of a Men’s Health Netherlands photoshoot—losing fat, adding visible muscle and finishing just 4 pounds lighter after 11 weeks.

The scales barely budged, but his body changed dramatically.

“The fitness industry has been telling you to pick one for decades,” says Sapstead. “Bulk first, cut later. Build the muscle, then reveal it.”

Sapstead accepts that fat loss requires an energy deficit, while building muscle requires energy. However, he says the apparent contradiction comes from treating your body like a single energy account.

“Fat tissue and muscle tissue operate through different pathways,” he explains. “You can be breaking down stored fat for fuel while simultaneously building muscle protein—as long as the conditions for muscle protein synthesis are met.”

Those conditions are relatively straightforward: enough protein and a sufficiently challenging resistance-training stimulus.

Sapstead points towards research examining simultaneous fat loss and muscle gain. According to Sapstead, the phenomenon appeared consistently across the research and wasn’t simply a beginner-only fluke.

He also references studies in which participants consumed between 400 and 800 additional calories each day, all from protein.

By conventional logic, those extra calories should have resulted in weight gain. Instead, Sapstead says the participants either maintained their weight or lost fat while gaining or preserving muscle.

“Body recomposition is real,” he concludes. “It’s well-supported, and for the right person in the right circumstances, it happens faster than most expect.”

Schadenberg had just 11 weeks to prepare for his photoshoot. He was running a business and raising a family—a familiar combination for many of us—that had gradually pushed training, nutrition, and recovery down his list of priorities.

“He’d let his training slip,” says Sapstead. “Not from a lack of drive, but through the entirely predictable reality of running a business and raising a family.”

His sleep was suffering, his diet lacked structure and he had no consistent exercise routine. Like many men in their late 30s and 40s, Sapstead says, he was also “chronically undereating protein.”

That might not sound like an ideal starting point, but it gave Schadenberg several powerful variables to improve almost immediately.

“Every one of those factors is a recomposition accelerant,” says Sapstead.

Returning to resistance training after a significant lay-off can produce a response closer to that of a beginner. The stimulus feels novel again, adaptations arrive quickly and previously built muscle may return faster than it took to develop in the first place.

Combine that with more protein, better recovery and structured training, and you can create the conditions to rebuild muscle while using stored body fat to help cover the energy costs.

“The body has been starved of the right inputs,” says Sapstead. “Give it protein, training and adequate recovery, and it responds.”

After 11 weeks, Schadenberg was only 4 pounds lighter. But his before-and-after photographs showed considerably more muscle and significantly less body fat.

“Fat came off. Muscle went on. Bodyweight barely moved,” says Sapstead.

Sapstead says recomposition is particularly well suited to anyone who has been away from consistent strength training, is carrying more body fat than they would like, habitually eats too little protein or has allowed sleep and recovery to deteriorate.

For experienced lifters who have trained intelligently, eaten well, and slept properly for years, the process is likely to be slower. There’s simply less low-hanging fruit.

For returning lifters, however, they're in a prime position for a recomp.

This isn’t the time for an aggressive diet or an uncontrolled bulk. Sapstead recommends eating around your maintenance calories or slightly above them, with approximately 200 to 300 additional calories coming predominantly from protein.

The aim is to provide enough energy to support training and muscle growth without creating a large surplus that encourages unnecessary fat gain.

Sapstead sets protein at around one gram per pound of bodyweight as a starting point, although higher intakes may also be appropriate.

Protein provides the raw materials required to repair and construct muscle tissue. It is also highly satiating, making it easier to control your overall food intake without constantly feeling hungry.

Perform three to four structured resistance-training sessions each week, with a focus on progressive overload.

Your body needs a reason to preserve and build muscle. That means gradually adding weight, completing more reps, improving your range of motion or producing better-quality work—not simply getting hot and tired doing random circuits, or going through the motions with zero intensity.

When fat is coming off while muscle is being added, your bodyweight may barely change. That doesn’t mean the approach has stopped working. It may mean it’s working exactly as intended.

“The scale would have told him nothing was happening,” Sapstead says of Schadenberg’s transformation. “The photos would have told him everything.”

Take progress pictures every two to three weeks, track your gym performance and pay attention to how your clothes fit. If your waist is shrinking, your strength is improving and you look more muscular, a stable bodyweight isn’t failure—it’s the holy grail of body recomp in action.

With almost 18 years in the health and fitness space as a personal trainer, nutritionist, breath coach and writer, Andrew has spent nearly half of his life exploring how to help people improve their bodies and minds.

As our fitness editor he prides himself on keeping Men’s Health at the forefront of reliable, relatable and credible fitness information, whether that’s through writing and testing thousands of workouts each year, taking deep dives into the science behind muscle building and fat loss or exploring the psychology of performance and recovery.

Whilst constantly updating his knowledge base with seminars and courses, Andrew is a lover of the practical as much as the theory and regularly puts his training to the test tackling everything from Crossfit and strongman competitions, to ultra marathons, to multiple 24 hour workout stints and (extremely unofficial) world record attempts.

#4781. Honda has dominated motorcycles for decades. Electric bikes are changing that

Honda has spent decades building one of the most dominant positions in the global motorcycle industry, selling millions of gasoline-powered two-wheelers each year. But in markets where electric motorcycles and scooters are becoming increasingly accessible, that dominance is starting to face a serious challenge.

Vietnam offers a particularly interesting case study, where rapidly growing electric motorcycle sales are beginning to reshape a market long dominated by Honda.

According to newly released nationwide sales figures, Vietnam saw more than 3 million motorcycle and scooter sales during the first nine months of 2026, representing 25.9% growth over the same period last year.

But the real story is in the electric segment, where sales surged 90.5% to reach 973,247 units. That means electric two-wheelers now account for approximately 32% of all new motorcycle and scooter sales in the country.

And the biggest beneficiary isn’t Honda. It’s actually Vietnamese electric vehicle manufacturer VinFast.

While Honda remains Vietnam’s largest motorcycle manufacturer overall, with sales growing 8.4% this year, VinFast has surged into second place with a staggering 152.1% increase in sales. Yamaha now sits in third place, followed by electric two-wheeler manufacturer Yadea in fourth.

Of the top four players, half are electric, and it’s precisely that half that is experiencing meteoric sales growth.

It’s an impressive reshuffling of a market that has traditionally been dominated by Japanese gasoline motorcycle manufacturers.

Vietnam’s transition hasn’t happened in a vacuum, either. Government efforts to reduce urban air pollution, including plans to restrict gasoline-powered motorcycles in parts of Hanoi, have helped create an increasingly favorable environment for electric alternatives.

Too bad for Honda but I'm thrilled to read about increasing sales of electric motorcycles. I don't live in or near Vietnam but the pollution from small gasoline engines affects everyone where the wind blows it.

And with companies like VinFast offering an expanding range of electric scooters and motorcycles, riders now have more practical alternatives to gasoline-powered models than ever before.

To be clear, Honda isn’t exactly struggling. Its motorcycle sales are still growing, and the Japanese giant remains the undisputed market leader in Vietnam. But its overall share of the market is shrinking, and its relatively modest growth compared to the exploding electric segment suggests that the market’s center of gravity is beginning to shift.

Vietnam may be just a single example, but it’s an important one of what can happen when electric two-wheelers become viable mainstream alternatives to gasoline motorcycles.

Honda has spent decades perfecting the gasoline motorcycle. The question now is how quickly it can adapt to a market that is increasingly interested in something else.

#4780. November skygazing: Planetary alignments, a supermoon, comet, and more

Published Oct 31, 2026 9:00 AM EDT

Autumn is here! The air is crisp, the leaves are falling, and the sky is alive. November brings a whole gamut of celestial phenomena for stargazing enthusiasts from a  planetary prom to a meteor shower that can explode occasionally into the most spectacular of sky shows, and  a comet that won’t return for 21 years Let’s get to it!

Mercury is generally difficult to spot. It’s our solar system’s smallest planet and is often lost in the sun’s haze. But in the middle of this month, this speedy boy is flitting in to join the party that Venus, Mars, and Jupiter are throwing all month. The three larger planets will be in alignment for all of November, festooning the morning sky just before  dawn. Venus will be in the southeastern sky, with Mars high in the eastern sky and Jupiter a bit lower, but also towards the east. And Mercury? Look low in the southeast, and it should be visible just before the sun emerges over the horizon.

As the month continues, Mars and Jupiter will edge closer and closer to one another, casting shy glances at one another across the sky like teenagers at a school dance. They’ll finally slide in for a waltz just before sunrise on November 16, where their conjunction in the eastern sky will be chaperoned by the bright star Regulus. Look to the east, but make sure you stop looking once the sun begins to peek its way into the firmament. No planetary conjunction is worth cooking your eyes.

And once the music stops and Mars and Jupiter will slip gracefully away, the fireworks will begin. The Leonids will be visible all month, but their peak is predicted for November 18. At that time, their radiant point—the point from which the meteors appear to emerge—will be right next to the two disengaging dancers in the constellation Leo. This shower usually produces 10 to 15 meteors per hour. However, in 1966 it exploded into one of the most spectacular displays of celestial pyrotechnics ever seen, with thousands of meteors visible every minute. So you never know what you might see!

This month’s full moon is the first of three consecutive supermoons. As per the ever-indispensable Farmer’s Almanac, it will reach peak illumination while below the horizon at 9:50 a.m. EST on November 24. When  actually visible, it’ll appear brightest on the evenings of November 23 and 24. This month’s moon takes its name from the industrious, dam-building rodents of North America, whose long summers of hard work start to pay off in November, when they retreat to their lodges to wait out the winter. Several other Indigenous nations have names that also refer to what animals get up to during the fall: the Tlingit call it the Digging Moon, to the Algonquin it’s the Whitefish Moon, while the Dakota and Lakota call it the Deer Rutting Moon.

The final event of November: a visit from Comet 161P/Hartley–IRAS. The space rock  will reach perihelion—the point at which it’s closest to the sun—on November 27. At that point, its magnitude will be about 12, which means you’ll want a decent telescope to spot it. The International Comet Quarterly suggests at least using a telescope with at least a 7.8 inch (20 centimeter) aperture. If you’ve got such an apparatus, look to the east-northeast, just above the horizon.

Remember that you’ll get the best experience gazing up at the stars if you get away from any sources of light pollution. You should also give your eyes plenty of time adjust to the darkness, and review our stargazing tips before heading out into the night.

#4779. I imported a $2,000 electric truck from China. Five years later, here’s the truth

Five years ago, I did something that seemed pretty ridiculous at the time. I bought a $2,000 electric mini-truck from China, had it shipped across the oceans to the US, and put it to work on my parents’ property in Florida.

The little white mini electric truck became something of an internet sensation, with my original unboxing and testing video quickly racking up over 10 million views, plus several million more from the follow-up videos.

It also attracted plenty of skeptics who were convinced that a $2,000 Chinese electric truck would fall apart within months, rust into oblivion, or otherwise prove to be a spectacular waste of money. “Good thing it has a bed,” was a common refrain. “So you can collect all the pieces that fall off along the way.”

I gave an update after the first year, showing that the truck was doing great. But to be fair, one year doesn’t tell us much.

Well now it’s been over five years, and I recently returned to Florida to see how the little truck has held up after five trips around the sun on my parents’ homestead. And I’ve got to say, the results are pretty surprising.

So here’s the truth about how the truck is doing five years later. Oh, and if you want to see it in action, you can check out my update video here. Trust me, you’ll want to.

First, it’s important to understand that this truck hasn’t spent five years sitting in a garage as some kind of novelty vehicle. It’s been a genuine workhorse on my parents’ 10-acre homestead.

Over the years, we’ve used it to haul everything from mulch and sand to lumber, tree branches, logs, yard waste, and everything in between.

Its hydraulic dump bed makes it particularly useful for moving bulk materials around the property, like hauling mulch and then dumping it in their raised planting beds.

My dad even uses it as a mobile irrigation truck during Florida’s dry season. I built him a solar-powered pump system that fills a water bladder in the truck’s bed with water from his pond, allowing him to drive around watering his trees and plants.

By now, it’s been involved in practically every major landscaping and construction project my parents have tackled.

We’ve also made some improvements over the years. Early on, my dad and I replaced the ridiculously stiff factory suspension springs with softer ones, making the ride considerably more comfortable. We added a custom tow hitch and swapped the original street tires for aggressive off-road tires that work much better on the property’s sandy and muddy terrain.

The suspension upgrade did reduce how much weight we can comfortably carry, though. Load more than around 500 pounds (220 kg) of sand or other bulk materials into the bed, and the rear end starts squatting enough that our homemade tow hitch threatens to touch grass.

But for most of the work we do, it’s been an excellent little utility vehicle.

And before anyone asks, no, this isn’t a street-legal truck. It was never really designed for American roads, and we use it almost exclusively on private property. Sure, it’s hit the pavement a few times since they live out in the boonies and its normal to see tractors and other non-street-legal vehicles on country roads, but it’s not the most ideal vehicle for long distance transport at 25 mph (40 km/h).

Here’s the part that surprised me most: Almost everything still works.

The electric windows still zip up and down with the speed of a guillotine. The electric door locks work. The headlights work. The backup camera works. Even the air conditioning still blows impressively cold air.

I actually checked that last one with a thermal camera during my latest visit, and the air coming out of the vents was around 55°F (12°C). Not bad for a five-year-old air conditioning system in a $2,000 truck!

The windshield wiper still operates, but its range of motion has decreased significantly. It now stops around the middle of the driver’s field of vision, which isn’t ideal when Florida’s famous afternoon thunderstorms roll through.

The rearview mirror has also developed an annoying habit of falling off. We’ve glued it back on multiple times, and it looks like another round of adhesive surgery is coming soon.

Inside, there’s some minor upholstery damage on the driver’s seat, including a few small tears and stressed seams in the cheap faux-leather material that you can see in the video.

The passenger seat, which sees much less use, still looks nearly new. In another few years, I might just swap the two seats to get another half decade or so out of them before we need some upholstery repair.

One decorative plastic panel around the driver’s door handle has popped off, though I still have the piece and could probably snap it back into place with a bit of effort. It’s just aesthetic though, so it’s been a low-priority repair.

And that’s pretty much the extent of the mechanical and electrical problems we’ve encountered.

There haven’t been any major drivetrain failures, the hydraulic dump bed still works, and the truck continues to start up and drive just as reliably as it did when it was new.

It still gets used for lots of bulk jobs, material hauling, and sometimes just random transportation around the property.

One of the biggest predictions from critics five years ago was that this cheap Chinese truck would quickly dissolve into a pile of rust.

To be fair, there is some rust. But nowhere near as much as you might expect.

Most of the corrosion is concentrated in areas where the paint has been scratched or chipped, especially around the tailgate and cargo bed.

The rustiest spot is definitely the top lip of the tailgate, where we usually have long objects hanging out of the bed, such as shovels, ladders, lumber, etc. The paint has worn through on that edge, and the rust has inevitably started in those few spots.

The truck is stored outdoors under a lean-to roof that I built between two shipping containers, but we have a skid-steer in front of it and so the rear of the truck sticks out and gets rained on several times a week (or several times a day during the summer).

We applied a paint-on bed liner during the truck’s first year, which helped protect the metal for quite a while.

After four years of hauling dirt, rocks, branches, and other abrasive materials though, that coating has started wearing through in a few places.

Every time I’m shoveling mulch out of the bed and I hear that scrape of metal on metal, I cringe just a bit before remembering that the truck cost me $2,000 and doesn’t owe me anything at this point.

Speaking of being parked outdoors with the rear hanging out for the world (and the UV) to see, there’s clearly an effect on the truck’s wear.

You can absolutely see the difference in the paint and plastic components. The front headlight lenses are still crystal clear, while the rear taillight lenses have become noticeably cloudy from UV exposure.

Despite that, the truck’s basic structure remains solid, and the rust is mostly cosmetic and limited to the high-impact areas that tend to get beaten up repeatedly, as you’d expect in any self-respecting work truck.

Considering that Florida combines high humidity, frequent rain, and intense sunshine, I’d call that a pretty impressive result for a vehicle that cost less than many electric bicycles.

Since the truck lives at my parents’ property, my dad has actually spent far more time using it than I have.

And when I asked him how he felt about the purchase after five years, he was surprisingly enthusiastic.

He described the truck as an incredibly functional piece of equipment that has become an essential part of maintaining the property.

In fact, he pointed out that the truck has been involved in virtually every significant project they’ve completed over the past five years.

It isn’t the only electric utility vehicle on the property anymore. My parents also have a Kandi electric UTV, which has taken over some of the smaller daily chores thanks to its better suspension and more convenient dump bed operation (the bed also lowers under power) which helps my dad lift the trash and recycling bins and drive them down the long private road to the street on pickup day.

But when it’s time to haul bulky loads, long branches, or large quantities of dirt and mulch, the Changli is still the vehicle of choice.

My dad also pointed out something that tends to get lost in discussions about cheap Chinese EVs: the operating costs have been almost nonexistent.

A full charge costs a little over a dollar in electricity, and the truck has required remarkably little maintenance over the years.

Even after five years, he says it still puts a smile on his face every time he drives it.

Yes, the truck cost me $2,000. Or technically, the price was $2,080.00, and that’s what I paid to the factory. At that point, it was mine.

Of course, it was still in China though, and so I had to pay an international freight company to have it sent on a cargo ship to the US (nearly $2,000 by itself, if I recall correctly).

Then I had to pay the US Treasury a bunch of tariffs to help make sure American automotive companies don’t have to compete with these types of vehicles.

And I also had to hire a customs broker to handle the import documentation for me, etc.

So there were several thousand dollars of additional fees on top of it, but I still think it was worth it based on the incredible amount of use it has given us over the years.

Of course, there’s an important caveat here for anyone considering getting a vehicle like this.

Remember, this is a very basic, low-speed electric utility vehicle without the safety equipment, crash protection, or regulatory approvals you’d expect from a modern full-size pickup truck.

It’s not something I’d recommend as a replacement for a road-going vehicle.

This is a work truck for us. It moves material, tows trailers and boats, carries the trash cans a quarter mile to the street each week, etc. In that way, as a private-property work truck, it’s been fantastic.

But even though I’m calling it simple, that doesn’t mean it wasn’t made pretty well. The truck has hauled countless loads, survived five years of rough Florida weather, and required very little maintenance. Even its cheap interior and basic electronics have held up better than I expected.

I also have to give some credit to the modifications we made early on, especially the suspension and tire upgrades, which turned a quirky little imported vehicle into something much more practical for off-road work.

The biggest unknown is how much longer it will last. Unfortunately, the truck doesn’t have a proper odometer, so I can’t even tell you how many miles we’ve accumulated over five years of driving around the property.

I also can’t tell you anything about battery degradation, since we don’t know how far it has driven (due to the lack of odometer), and the fact that even on 10 acres, you just can’t get that far from an outlet. We generally charge the 6 kWh battery every couple weeks just to keep it topped up, but range was never an issue and hasn’t become one, at least not for our use case. If you needed to drive this thing to the next town over each day, it could be another story.

Nothing like being forced to drive massive four-door trucks that weigh as much as four cars because your country is protecting monopolist manufacturers and only allows their land yachts for sale.

Basically, there’s no indication that the mini-truck is nearing the end of its useful life.

My dad thinks it could easily serve another five or even ten years, and after seeing how well it’s survived its first five, I’m inclined to agree that there’s plenty of life left in it.

When I first bought this thing, plenty of people told me it was a terrible idea. Five years later, with the truck still hauling dirt, carrying branches, and generally earning its keep, I’m feeling pretty good about that decision. It’s done a lot more in its five years than many “real” pickup trucks do in their entire lives.

Not bad for a funny little electric truck from China.

#4778. 3 things you might not know about daylight saving time

Published Oct 31, 2026 1:39 PM EDT

Heads up: The clocks are about to change. The evening of Halloween gets an extra hour as the clocks fall back an hour, meaning you can sleep in on Sunday, November 1.

Complaints about daylight savings are as old as daylight savings itself, and pretty much everyone has an opinion about the practice. As with any such topic, there are all kinds of myths and misunderstandings out there.

This one comes up a lot: the idea that farmers are the reason we have daylight savings. In this version of the story, farmers, who work outside and need to align their workdays with the daylight, were the ones who made the argument for the practice.

In truth, farmers were the main group opposed to daylight savings during World War I. According to the Library of Congress: “The agriculture industry fervently opposed the measure because farming schedules are based on sunrise and sunset not the clock.”

After the war there was a bill to repeal daylight savings, which passed through both houses of Congress. President Woodrow Wilson vetoed that bill, and his statement about the veto acknowledged this wouldn’t make farmers happy.

“I realize the very considerable and in some respects very serious inconveniences to which the daylight-saving law subjects the farmers of the country,” he wrote. Wilson sided with the industrial sector. The veto was overridden, leading to a long period where daylight savings was practiced only in certain areas. For example: New York City observed daylight savings, but rural areas in New York State did not (not what you’d expect if farmers broadly supported daylight savings).

None of this is to say that some farmers don’t support daylight savings time today—it’s just that farmers aren’t the reason the practice exists in America. If anything, they tried to stop it.

There are some “facts” repeated so often that hardly anyone questions them, and “Ben Franklin invented daylight savings time” remains one of them. The problem is that it’s not true.

I’d understand if you’re skeptical—I’m a Canadian journalist trying to steal an achievement from one of America’s founding fathers. But you don’t have to take my word on this one—The Franklin Institute, a museum dedicated to Franklin’s legacy, states that “Daylight saving time is one thing that Franklin did not invent.” The United States didn’t even implement daylight savings until 1918, well over a century after Franklin passed away.

So where did the idea that he invented it come from? Probably from a satirical Journal de Paris article Franklin penned back in 1784.

In that piece he jokingly encouraged the residents of Paris to wake up earlier in the morning, in order to spend less money on candles. He also proposed a tax on shutters, rationing of candles, a prohibition of carriages on the streets after sunset, and church bells ringing at the crack of dawn every day. He, it goes without saying, wasn’t being entirely serious.

So where did the idea for daylight savings come from? New Zealand entomologist George Hudson first proposed intentionally shifting the clock in an 1895 talk to the Wellington Philosophical Society, then followed up with a paper in 1898.

This isn’t a myth, exactly, but it is something that rarely comes up in contemporary discussions about daylight savings. Multiple US states have proposed doing away with standard time entirely. Nationally, the Sunshine Protection Act, which passed the House over the summer, would institute the change from sea to shining sea.

Here’s the thing, though: this isn’t the first time. The US tried making daylight savings permanent during the height of the 1970s energy crisis. The problem was that people hated it. What was supposed to be a two-year experiment lasted less than a year because of a massive change in public opinion.

Support for the change started high, as an October 1974 New York Times article lays out: 79 percent of the public favored the idea in December of 1973, but by February of 1974, that dropped to 42 percent—a 37-point swing. A bill to restore standard time in winter passed the House by a 362 to 16 vote.

What caused the backlash? Dark winter mornings. Particularly prominent were complaints from parents, who didn’t like their children walking to school in the dark.

A 1975 study by the US Department of Transportation concluded that a year-round switch possibly isn’t a great idea, proposing instead a schedule change. “We conclude that modest overall benefits might be realized by a shift from the historic 6-month DST system (May through October) to an 8-month DST system (March through October),” the paper concludes. This, notably, is pretty much what the US has been doing since 2007.

The past isn’t a prediction of the future—it’s possible switching to year-round daylight savings would go differently today. Walking to school is less common, for one thing, and streets are better lit. All the same, it’s worth realizing this has been tried before.

#4777. 3 Real Ways to Evolve Past Your Trust Issues

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Trust forms the basis of all our connections. When trust is strong, relationships flourish, communication is transparent, and individuals feel safe and valued. On the other hand, a lack of trust can lead to emotional distance, misunderstandings, and even the breakdown of relationships.

Despite the pivotal role of trust, many people struggle to place their faith in others, often due to past betrayals. These experiences of disappointment can create a reluctance to trust new people, forming a barrier in the development of meaningful relationships. A study published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology underscores how trust influences memory. People with low trust in their partner tend to recall the partner’s mistakes negatively, emphasizing self-protection over relationship dependence. Conversely, those with high trust exhibit a positive bias when remembering their partner’s transgressions.

However, letting fear dictate our ability to trust can hinder personal growth and prevent the development of meaningful relationships.

While we cannot control the betrayals of others, there are actions we can take proactively to develop a robust understanding and sense of trust so that we can be generous yet mindful the next time we decide to trust someone with it. Here are three.

Distrust in others often arises when you repeatedly break your own commitments. Think about it: If you can’t trust yourself to keep the promises you make to yourself, how can you trust others to keep their promises to you? To begin trusting others, start by honoring your word to yourself.

Another source of the fear of trusting others is the dread of judgment and criticism. What you fear others might critique about you often mirrors your self-criticism. Low self-esteem and self-doubt can hinder trust in others. To build trust with others, you must first learn to fully accept and love yourself.

It’s easy to remain guarded and skeptical, but trust cannot be developed without taking the risk of trusting others. Trust is a two-way street that requires effort and vulnerability. Here’s how you can start trusting by actually trusting:

While you are at it, be prepared for the possibility of disappointment. Not every person or situation will result in a positive outcome. Instead of dwelling on disappointments, view them as learning experiences that can refine your judgment in the future and be open to the potential for trustful connections.

Trust is the bedrock of any healthy relationship, but fear often prevents us from placing our faith in others. Building self-trust is an incremental process; it won’t happen overnight. But by taking proactive steps, you can break down the barriers that keep you from forming deep and meaningful connections. Building trust is a journey, and the rewards of stronger, more fulfilling relationships are well worth the effort.

A new 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 9C1 police pursuit vehicle (PPV) was on display in the GM Fleet booth at the Orange County Convention Center this past week, where the new half-ton was featured fitted a new, 402 hp version of the venerable 5.7 small-block Chevy V8 sending 428 lb-ft of torque to both axles through a 10-speed automatic transmission.
