#4704. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: What Breast Cancer Patients Need When Treatment Ends

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Supporting your health & well-being at every stage of your breast cancer journey

Resources to support your emotional health and well-being

Tips for nourishing your body and mind while living with breast cancer

Navigating your next steps after diagnosis

A guide to medications, treatments, and procedures for breast cancer

Guide to symptoms, tests, and screenings for early detection

Resources to support you during remission or recurrence

Breast cancer awareness has never been higher. Every October, the world turns pink and the key messages—that early diagnosis saves lives and that knowing the risk factors reduces the risk—are hard to miss.

Breast cancer remains the leading cause of cancer death amongst women in most countries, with an estimated 694,000 deaths annually and around 8.2 million women globally living with a breast cancer diagnosis, according to 2024 data from the World Health Organization (WHO)’s Global Health Observatory.

But when October ends, and the wall-to-wall campaigns move on, what has awareness actually changed for those impacted by breast cancer?

For Marisa Weiss, MD, the answer is that there is always more to be done, and she’s uniquely placed to hold that view.

Dr. Weiss has treated breast cancer patients for more than 30 years. In 2000, she founded Breastcancer.org, a not-for-profit that provides expert-reviewed medical and lifestyle information on breast health and breast cancer to millions of people globally.

Sixteen years ago, she was diagnosed with stage 1 breast cancer, becoming, in her own words, a “dual citizen” in that moment, with lived experience on both sides of the doctor’s desk.

I had the pleasure of sitting down with Dr. Weiss as part of Healthline’s Breast Cancer Awareness Month coverage to talk about how awareness has changed care for the better for millions of people around the world, but why critical gaps remain, and how access to trusted information and community can help close those gaps.

“It’s good that awareness is high, but knowledge remains low,” she said. The misconception she sees most is the belief that breast cancer is something that happens to other families.

“Most people think they’re off the hook because it doesn’t run in their family,” Dr. Weiss explained. In fact, 85%-90% of people who get breast cancer have no known family history and no known gene in the family, “so we’re all at risk,” she warns.

For most, a diagnosis arrives as a shock. “They’re completely surprised, flattened by it. Their life is upside down, and they scramble to find what they need to know,” Dr. Weiss noted.

That aftershock caused by a diagnosis is at the core of why Breastcancer.org exists. Because the person whose life is at stake is increasingly expected to direct their own care and advocate for their needs, access to accurate and empowering information is critical in that process. “Decisions aren’t being made around the patient and for the patient in a bubble,” Dr. Weiss said. “Decision-making is supposed to be shared.”

With appointments hard to get and clinicians stretched, she said patients have to do more of the work.

In practice, Dr. Weiss says that means preparing by writing down your family history on both sides and making sure your care team knows who you are. “What’s important to you? Who’s in your life? Do you want more children? Are you planning a vacation? All those decisions can have an impact on the care you receive.”

Where Dr. Weiss sees the widest gap is after treatment ends. Speaking from personal experience, she said: “I had the best care possible, and there were still gaps. You can find yourself alone with lots of questions and fears.”

Understandably, a great deal of focus and attention is centered on diagnosis and treatment, she said. Then it stops. “When your life is supposed to go back to normal, it never does. You have to find a new normal. That quiet phase can be really lonely and difficult.”

For Dr. Weiss, the questions that fill that silence are often as practical as they are emotional: “How do I know my treatment is working? How do I tell leftover side effects from new ones? How do I go back to work, and who do I tell? How do I talk to my kids? What about that new treatment I heard about on TV last night?”

That post-treatment period can also be the first time anyone has really had a chance to stop, take stock, and start asking “what next?”

“You might think, what happened to me? Who do I want to be moving forward? How do I have a long life full of wonderful things, and remain as independent as possible?”

Some of what patients do post-care never reaches their doctor at all, with Dr. Weiss pointing to a growing amount of personal care happening outside the hospital: GLP-1s, peptides, hormonal therapies, supplements, medical cannabis, to name a few. Breastcancer.org’s annual Pulse survey shows that people reported being interested in all of those things and more, and that they tend to learn about them online rather than risk the stigma of bringing them up with their doctors.

“They don’t really trust that their doctor knows much about these things,” she said, “and they don’t want a conversation that makes them feel judged. Some patients worry about what ends up in their medical record and then everyone’s going to know.”

Dr. Weiss says the stakes are real, because some of those choices can interact with cancer medications with potential for adverse or unexpected side effects. “That is why people turn to Breastcancer.org with questions that are personal, private, and important, including “what do I need to share with my doctor, and who’s on a need-to-know basis?”

Peer communities fill part of that gap. “Breastcancer.org’s members share medical information, tips, and practical advice with people who have just had the call, or are about to start treatment and don’t know what to expect,” Dr. Weiss shared, and said that while she values that kind of support system hugely, it does come with a caveat:

The same community can also be intrusive. Dr. Weiss describes standing at a party, drink in hand, when someone asks what kind of cancer you had, what you did, and whether it came back. Her advice to patients, which she took herself: “Put up your hand and say, ‘thank you so much for caring, but I cannot hear another story right now.’”

On the topic of AI and its impact on treatment and care, Dr. Weiss is cautiously optimistic. On the treatment front, she points to tools that help radiologists read mammograms more thoroughly and assess future risk as game changers in the fight against breast cancer.

Breastcancer.org also uses AI for tasks such as finding citations and interpreting pathology reports. But like many, she is wary of misinformation. “When you’re fearful, you look for reassurance, and you don’t want to be reassured by misinformation. When it comes to health information, every word matters.”

Her final advice is for the appointment itself, which she says she has even struggled with. “When they start speaking quickly in complex medical language, you can get lost really fast. The risk is you kind of fake it. That must not happen.”

“Do your research in advance. Write things down. Bring someone you trust as a second set of ears. Ask direct questions. Don’t worry if it sounds funny or silly. It’s always a smart question when you are dealing with your health.” Just be prepared for the questions to multiply from there. “Once you get a certain set of questions answered, that raises more questions. So just write it all down.”

If breast cancer has touched your life, know that you are not alone. Healthline’s Bezzy Breast Cancer Community is a space for peer support, feel-good stories, and advice in a welcoming, stigma-free environment when your lived experience is seen, heard and valued.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Saturday in our Healthline Daily newsletter. He’ll soon be launching a dedicated Letter from the Editor newsletter coming to an inbox near you later in the fall.

#4703. Maximo milestone: friendly robot has completed 300,000 tasks

After completing the first half of Amazon’s Bellefield complex last summer, Maximo engineers have put their helpful robot friend into high gear, with the latest version 3.0 robot-equipped construction crews installing as many as 24 solar panel modules per hour, per person. And now, the company is reporting that Maximo has completed its 300,000th construction task. (!)

If that 24 modules per hour, per person rate sounds fast, that’s because it is. At full tilt, the latest Maximo robot-equipped crews have nearly doubled the output of traditional installation methods at similar solar locations throughout Southern California. Now, with 300,000 tasks under its belt, the robot is proving to be both fast and durable.

“The future of solar construction depends on bringing together the experience of our people and new technology,” explains Matt Tetrault, President of Primoris’ Renewables business.

Like just about everyone these days, Maximo is playing up its machines’ NVDIVIA hardware, re-branding its robots’ repetitive automation as “physical AI.” That’s not to say the robots don’t work, however – as their deployment at Amazon’s Bellefield solar field is proving.

(By) leveraging NVIDIA AI infrastructure together with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries and NVIDIA Isaac Sim open robotics simulation framework, the Maximo team was able to develop, test and refine robotic capabilities through physics-based simulation and AI driven modeling before deploying updates in the field. The combination of AI, vision, robotics and simulation driven engineering reduced development and validation timelines and increased confidence in field performance as the robotic fleet scaled.

Amazon Web Services (AWS) powered the development, deployment, and operation of Maximo’s AI-driven field systems. AWS provides scalable computing, automated software delivery, and advanced data analytics, including real-time construction intelligence, enabling Maximo to collect operational robotics data and continuously improve performance.

The rapid deployment of solar panels at utility scale projects like this one, which is set to eventually reach over a GW of solar generating capacity, will help companies like Amazon reduce their carbon footprint, of course – but also save them big money as the price of fossil fuels continues to climb.

So Primoris’ Renewables is the name of a business, Maximo is the name of a solar robotics company incubated by The AES Corporation. Maximo makes a robot (also called Maximo I think) using NVDIVIA hardware and software, and also AWS cloud software, and Bellefield is a solar field owned by Amazon. Or so I gather so far.

The Maximo team says it has plans to extend its robots potential use cases beyond solar and into construction tasks that require similar pick and place and feeding and attaching movements, site logistics, and site cleanup. And like just about every other business that demands a high degree of physical labor, the construction industry is facing huge labor shortages, making machines like Maximo that provide real efficiency gains welcome additions to the job site.

#4702. Beyond 'Forgive and Forget': 5 Practical Relationship Habits

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

In an era dominated by relationship burnout and hyper-individualism, many couples find themselves trapped in endless cycles of friction and emotional distance. Breaking free requires adopting habits that run counter to modern culture. Here are some counterintuitive relationship habits you could consider adopting or adapting to fit the unique rhythm and idiosyncrasies of your (current or future) intimate relationship.

Life is a process of displacement. When you are born, you immediately become #1. As long as you are single, you remain #1—it’s still about you and your freedom.

When you get married, you become #2. You have to learn to put your spouse first (without compromising your deeply held values—that’s why choosing the right person is the most important decision you’ll ever make) if you want the marriage to work.

When you have a child, you become #3. By the time you become a grandparent, you’re lucky if you’re still in the Top 10.

While it sounds like you become weaker, it’s the opposite: You become stronger. While it sounds like you become a follower, it’s, again, the opposite: This is true leadership. The front-stage star is not a leader, but a showman—not the director, but an actor.

The true leader is the one you don’t see, the back-stage architect whose undying devotion enables the unfolding drama, which involves many, to captivate and enthrall, night after night.

Twenty-five years ago, I was wrestling with my inner demons about commitment and went on a walk along the Potomac River outside of Washington, DC, with a close family friend who had been married to his wife for more than 40 years.

“How have you managed being married for so long?” I asked him.

Robert looked at the turbulent rapids and thought for a while. Then he said, “The best advice I ever received was from my aunt, while I was fixing my tuxedo just before Charlene and I were married.”

“She said, ‘Robert, always remember this: Whatever Charlene does, just give. No matter what happens, always give. And the two of you will be fine.’”

I’ll pass on Robert’s aunt’s sage advice: Just give. No matter what. It’s your only power. You control how, when, and what to give.

What you receive, on the other hand, is completely out of your control. Yet the more and better you give, the more love will also come in your direction.

In other words, let things go. There are two things you do in life: You choose how you want to live, and you live with what you choose.

You chose a long-term commitment to this person, which means letting lots of things (but not everything) go. Consider that the opposite of forgiveness is resentment. A word derived from the Latin roots re (again) and sentire (to feel), resentment is to feel anger again and again until you become paralyzed.

Forgiveness is a better option: while resentment paralyzes, forgiveness liberates.

As children, we’re often told by adults—generally with good intentions—to “forgive and forget.” To forget, however, may not be the best idea.

If you fall into a ditch, the last thing you want to do is forget the location of the ditch. Such a strategy may result in your falling in again.

A better way to approach forgiveness is to acknowledge what the other person did, file it away, give for the other person to yourself, and then let it go. This approach need not include your tolerating the same behavior again.

Forgiveness, in fact, does not necessarily lead to a continued relationship. In many cases, forgiveness enables you to detach yourself from the relationship, not only physically but also emotionally and psychologically.

Importantly, while trust binds, forgiveness releases. While forgiveness is needed for personal development, trust is needed for relational development.

Trust is not necessarily an evolutionary adaptive behavior, as it can lead to more harmful behavior from the other person. A man can apologize to his wife for an affair, for example, regain her trust, and then continue to cheat on her afterward.

While trusting a specific person whom you feel has harmed you is not necessary for your evolution as a human being, forgiving them is. Forgiveness is one of your most critical attributes because until you let go of your suffering, you don’t let it recede from the present and into the past.

Until you forgive and then learn to love any person in your life, you remain trapped in a drama with them. You remain on their stage, entangled in an invisible thread that binds you to them.

You may be acting out the drama with the surrogates you bring into your life to replace them, but you are still cast in the role. This is how love liberates, how love sets you free.

The more you are able to take this cognitive step toward understanding and respecting innate differences that will always be beyond your control, the more inner peace and happiness you will invite into your life.

If you are like most of us, you probably have not yet made this transformative decision. You have likely spent most of your life preoccupied with the comings and goings and machinations and preferences of the other characters in your story—including and especially your partner—instead of seeing them as they are: as other human beings who enter and exit your stage throughout your life.

How can you accept yourself and others as you and they are while also retaining your optimism about what you and they can become?

#4701. Relaxed bear wins award for luxurious eating style—underneath an Alaskan waterfall

Published Nov 4, 2026 11:13 AM EST

Typically, when a bear catches a nutritious salmon, they don’t eat it under a rushing waterfall. But one unnamed black bear (Ursus americanus) eating at Anan Creek in Alaska’s Tongass National Forest decided to park underneath a waterfall and enjoy his fishy snack.

For this culinary innovation, the U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest has awarded the unnamed bear with the 2026 Shower Beer award.

“After watching this relaxed black bear gnawing on a salmon under rushing waters, we’re wondering if it might catch on—like the ursine equivalent of the shower beer,” the team writes. “The more you watch, the more sense it makes. No mess and no need to move to start fishing again. This bear may be on to something.”

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Like their beefy counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return annually each summer to eat salmon and teach their cubs how to fish and survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted here, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their behavior.

#4700. Former CAKE team is back in the kitchen with a new electric motorcycle

If the new ReBake Abler electric motorcycle looks like it might share a bit of DNA with Sweden’s dearly departed CAKE, there’s a good reason for that.

ReBake Motors has officially unveiled its first electric two-wheeler at EICMA 2026 in Milan, introducing the Abler as a highly modular, utility-focused electric moped and light motorcycle.

Behind the new Swedish company is founder and CEO Karl Ytterborn, who spent eight years at CAKE from its founding in 2016 through 2024. CAKE famously built some of the most interesting minimalist electric motorcycles and utility bikes on the market before ultimately collapsing after failing to secure additional funding. Ytterborn says ReBake is intended to apply many of the lessons learned during that experience, while eliminating unnecessary cost and complexity.

Its chunky 42mm aluminum tube frame isn’t just a styling exercise. ReBake designed it as a mounting system, allowing cargo accessories to attach directly to the frame at multiple locations. That means riders can configure the bike for everything from carrying groceries and passengers to more serious utility duties.

There are two versions. The Abler45 is an EU L1e-B moped with a 45 km/h (28 mph) top speed, 4 kW nominal motor and 5.12 kW peak output. It starts at €3,990 including VAT.

The €4,990 Abler80 steps up to the A1 light motorcycle category, increasing nominal power to 6.14 kW and peak power to 7.68 kW while pushing the top speed beyond 80 km/h (50 mph). Both versions use a direct-drive rear hub motor.

Energy comes from removable 2 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries weighing 17 kg (37.5 lb) apiece. The Abler45 comes standard with one battery but can carry two, while the Abler80 includes two for 4 kWh of total capacity. With both batteries, ReBake claims up to 160 km (99 miles) of low-speed urban range on the Abler45 or 114 km (71 miles) on the Abler80. Each battery can be charged either on or off the bike from a normal 230V outlet, reaching a full charge in four hours.

The rest of the hardware includes 14-inch cast wheels, 140mm of front suspension travel, dual rear shocks, front and rear disc brakes with combined braking, regenerative braking, and full LED lighting.

Perhaps more interesting than any individual specification, though, is simply seeing another Swedish electric motorcycle startup emerge from CAKE’s ashes.

CAKE demonstrated that there was plenty of appetite for unconventional, lightweight electric motorcycles. Unfortunately, it also demonstrated just how difficult it is to turn that enthusiasm into a sustainable business.

ReBake appears to be getting another crack at that equation – this time with eight years’ worth of lessons already baked in.

#4699. Women With Autoimmune Diseases More Likely to Be Misdiagnosed Than Men

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new international study found that women with autoimmune diseases often experience longer delays in getting a correct diagnosis compared to men.

The research, published in eClinicalMedicine on October 12, also shows that females report higher rates of being misdiagnosed, especially with mental health or psychosomatic conditions.

These findings highlight challenges in diagnosing autoimmune diseases and suggest that sex differences affect patients’ experiences in healthcare.

This is significant given that autoimmune diseases, conditions in which the body’s immune system attacks its own healthy cells, are estimated to affect around 4.6% of the U.S. population. Additionally, despite the observed disparities in diagnoses, women are almost two times as likely as men to be diagnosed with an autoimmune disease.

Researchers conducted an online survey between December 7, 2024, and March 7, 2025, inviting adults ages 18 and older who had a confirmed autoimmune or rheumatic disease.

The survey was carefully designed and tested with input from patients, charities, and medical experts to ensure it captured important information about patients’ diagnostic journeys.

Participants were asked about the time it took from when they first noticed symptoms to when they received their autoimmune diagnosis.

They also reported how many healthcare visits they made before diagnosis and whether they felt their symptoms were ever misdiagnosed as mental health issues, psychosomatic problems (physical symptoms caused or worsened by psychological factors), or another physical disease.

The survey was widely shared on social media, patient support groups, and community organizations to reach a broad audience.

Special efforts were made to include underrepresented groups such as males, younger individuals, and people from minority ethnic backgrounds.

The survey was available in five languages, and participants could complete it with help from researchers if needed.

To analyze the data, the team used statistical methods, adjusting for factors like age, type of autoimmune disease, continent of residence, and financial situation.

These methods helped compare the experiences of males and females while accounting for differences in disease types and other factors

The study included 6,607 participants, with 91.2% identifying as female and most living in the United Kingdom. On average, women were younger than men in the study.

Autoimmune thyroid disease was the most common condition reported. Non-autoimmune conditions like anxiety were more commonly reported by women, while men reported higher rates of hypertension.

One of the main findings was that women reported longer delays before getting a diagnosis. Nearly 32% of females experienced delays of four years or more from symptom onset to diagnosis, compared to about 26% of males.

On the other hand, men were more likely to be diagnosed within a year of symptom onset (nearly 50% of males versus 40% of females).

Women also made more visits to healthcare providers before diagnosis, with 26.2% having 11 or more visits compared to 18.4% of men.

When it came to misdiagnoses, women were significantly more likely to report that their symptoms had been mistaken for mental health issues (43.3% of females vs. 32.7% of males) or psychosomatic causes (33.9% of females vs. 21.5% of males).

However, there was no significant difference between men and women in being misdiagnosed with another physical disease.

The type of autoimmune disease also influenced misdiagnosis rates. Diseases with clear physical symptoms or definitive lab tests, like type 1 diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis, had lower rates of mental health and psychosomatic misdiagnoses.

In contrast, conditions such as autoimmune encephalitis or undifferentiated connective tissue disease had higher rates of these misdiagnoses (over 50%).

After adjusting for disease type and other factors, women still had higher odds of reporting mental health or psychosomatic misdiagnoses compared to men.

Other factors affected misdiagnosis rates, too. People living in continents outside the United Kingdom, those with lower household income, and certain disease groups were more likely to report psychiatric or psychosomatic misdiagnoses. Age, however, was not linked to the risk of being misdiagnosed.

Muhammad Qasim, MD, a pulmonologist and medical writer with MySleepApneaTeam, told Healthline that autoimmune diseases are often difficult to diagnose. Qasim wasn’t involved in the study.

“Early symptoms can be vague, fluctuate over time, and affect several parts of the body,” he said. “Fatigue, pain, sleep problems, brain fog, and mood changes do not immediately point to one diagnosis.”

Qasim echoed the study’s findings, explaining that similar symptoms may be interpreted differently in women versus men, with complaints being attributed to anxiety, stress, or psychosomatic causes.

However, there are probably multiple factors contributing to this phenomenon, he said.

“Differences in disease presentation, gaps in research, fragmented care, and unconscious bias can all contribute,” said Qasim. “Once a psychiatric explanation enters the medical record, there is also a risk that later clinicians view new symptoms through that same lens.”

Regarding unconscious bias, the study’s authors noted that women have historically been treated by doctors as “less credible” and more “emotional” in reporting their symptoms, which can influence how doctors interpret them.

These disparities in diagnosis are important, however, because longer waits and erroneous diagnoses can delay proper treatment and increase women’s frustration, leading them to stop asking for help.

The researchers suggest that healthcare providers need to be aware of these concerns and consider autoimmune diseases carefully when patients, especially females, present with more complicated symptoms.

Adam Carewe, MD, a physician in Boulder, CO, and a clinical informaticist with General Medicine who wasn’t involved in the study, offered guidance to those experiencing symptoms on how to obtain a proper diagnosis.

Healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.

“Patients can keep an accurate symptom timeline, bring in family history, ask what else could be explaining these symptoms, ask for a plan for next steps if initial testing/treatment, do not change anything, and lastly get a second opinion,” he advised.

Carewe emphasized the value of not giving up on finding answers. “The most important thing for anyone with persistent symptoms of any kind is to continue to work with your primary care clinician and continue to advocate for yourself,” he said.

#4698. Man builds robotic cat feeder that senses when dish is empty

Published Nov 4, 2026 12:00 PM EST

Pet owners can pick from any number of automatic cat feeders at this point, and even shell out hundreds of dollars for a particularly fancy kit. But at the end of the day, most of them are simply a scooper that dumps out premeasured amounts of feline food based on an internal timer.

Jason Winfield, a New Zealand-based YouTuber and frequent traveler, wanted a slightly more advanced option: a robotic cat feeder that distributes a predetermined amount of food for his two pals, and also senses when the dish is actually empty.

“I tried a few of those automatic feeders off-the-shelf, and look, they’re fine. They do the job. Sort of,” Winfield explains in his recent video. “But here’s what bothered me: How do I know my cat actually ate?”

Winfield’s invention is designed to avoid overfeeding or accidentally building a mountain of kibble. The device runs on a Raspberry Pi Pico with Wi-Fi capabilities, and includes a tiny LCD screen and a buzzer to alert when food has been delivered. An onboard real-time clock (RTC) module keeps time even without direct power, which allows for a timed feeding window for daily rations.

Winfield also attached a 3D-printed cat head toggle to cycle through settings on the feeder’s screen. DIY projects like this are bound to run into errors, so Winfield also encoded a failsafe that turns off the feed dispenser if the dish has remained full for a specific length of time.There’s even an ultrasonic sensor to detect the presence of a cat, so the feeder doesn’t inadvertently drop kibble on their head.

The end result is an efficient, reliable automatic feeder that keeps Winfield’s cats happy. Winfield himself is even confident that his cats will never go hungry while he’s traveling.

#4697. The Benefits of Having an Older Sibling During Adolescence

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Adolescence is an important time when young people seek independence from their parents, focusing on friends and romantic partners and figuring out who they want to be. As teens navigate these important developmental tasks, they will learn and grow with the help of others. For adolescents with an older sibling, that sibling can be an important, trusted family resource who helps guide them during this developmental period.

While siblings do spend less time together during adolescence, their relationship remains important and influential for youths' social, emotional, and cognitive development. In fact, adolescents report sharing and discussing personal information and thoughts with their siblings daily. Although older siblings are not always a positive influence, they can play a beneficial role in the lives of younger siblings during adolescence.

In the United States, most siblings are about two years apart in age, creating likely similarities in their life experiences. These similarities, along with siblings’ shared family history and special understanding of one another, can make an older sibling an ideal resource during adolescence. A sibling can also provide an alternative source of support for youth who may not feel comfortable talking to their parents or need a different perspective.

Teens may also seek out their older siblings as relatable confidants, perhaps using them as a sounding board before approaching their parents or other adults. Adolescents may enjoy the back-and-forth conversation with their sibling more than top-down pressure from parents. Reflecting this trust, research shows that adolescent siblings frequently talk about their daily activities, media use, nonfamilial relationships, academics, and future plans.

During adolescence, sibling support is often mutual, especially when navigating family matters. However, older siblings generally have more influence on younger siblings than vice versa, often adopting a teacher or mentor role even if they are only a few years older. Younger siblings often admire and look up to their older siblings. This status typically happens because of birth order and age: Older siblings are likely to face social situations with peers and romantic partners, encounter academic challenges and classes, and make decisions about future plans before their younger siblings.

Does it matter if an adolescent has an older brother or sister? The findings are mixed, with some studies showing no effect. Other studies show that younger siblings receive more guidance and support from same-sex rather than opposite-sex older siblings. This is thought to happen because same-sex siblings share greater similarities and relate to each other more easily. Additionally, older sisters are often close confidants and mentors for younger sisters and provide more advice than older brothers do. For example, one study found that older sisters give younger sisters specific instructions and information about dating and romantic relationships.

Older siblings can influence adolescent younger siblings in several ways, including by guiding them through direct instruction and encouragement or by providing information and advice. Another way older siblings influence younger siblings is by serving as role models. By watching their older siblings’ activities, choices, and subsequent consequences, younger siblings learn from them.

Older brothers and sisters are invaluable guides promoting positive development for their less experienced younger siblings in a variety of areas, including dating and peer relationships, body image, and prosocial skills like empathy. One study showed that older siblings shape adolescents’ social skills and their athletic and artistic interests, particularly when older siblings excelled in those areas. Other work found that how much adolescents discussed extracurricular activities, media, and academics with their older siblings was linked to their success in friendships, sports, and school.

Parents can encourage strong, loving sibling relationships in which older siblings serve as positive role models and resources for younger siblings during adolescence through the following suggestions:

Killoren, S. E., & Roach, A. L. (2014). Sibling conversations about dating and sexuality: Sisters as confidants, sources of support, and mentors. Family Relations, 63(2), 232–243. https://doi.org/10.1111/fare.12057

Tucker, C. J., & Winzeler, A. (2007). Adolescent siblings’ daily discussions: Connections to perceived academic, athletic, and peer competency. Journal of Research on Adolescence, 17(1), 145–152. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1532-7795.2007.00515.x

Whiteman, S. D., & Christiansen, A. (2008). Processes of sibling influence in adolescence: Individual and family correlates. Family Relations, 57(1), 24–34. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1741-3729.2007.00480.x

#4696. Walking, Yoga, or Zumba? Which Exercises Help Relieve Menopause Mood Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Physical activity may help support mood and improve quality of life during the menopause transition, according to a study published on October 13 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society.

This review of 12 clinical trials involving over 1,000 people ages 40 to 65 found that both aerobic and mind-body exercises may be associated with reduced depressive symptoms and improved well-being.

It is common for individuals to experience psychological symptoms during menopause, including depression, anxiety, low mood, stress, and difficulty with thinking and memory. These symptoms can have a significant effect on quality of life, with an estimated 1 in 10 women leaving work due to menopause symptoms.

This study found that regular physical activity may help improve certain psychological symptoms and overall quality of life during menopause.

The types of physical activity in the review were broken into two categories: aerobic-based exercise (ABIs) and mind-body activities (MBAs).

The researchers found that ABIs showed the strongest effects on reducing depressive symptoms and improving overall quality of life. This may be particularly relevant during perimenopause when women may be more vulnerable to mood instability due to estrogen fluctuations.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, pointed out that there are various ways that ABIs can have positive effects.

Ross explained that aerobic exercise may help improve menopausal symptoms through several mechanisms, including the release of endorphins, reduced inflammation, improved cholesterol levels, and better regulation of body temperature and sleep cycles.

MBAs were shown to have a greater effect on improving psychological quality of life. These exercises involve mindfulness, body awareness, and breathwork. They may help improve emotional regulation.

ABIs tended to require fewer sessions. This may mean these types of exercises are easier to fit in, especially if you are facing time or energy constraints. For example, in one trial, participants were instructed to walk for 30 minutes, three times per week. In another trial, participants attended three hour-long Zumba classes per week.

In contrast, one trial using MBAs instructed participants to attend two 75-minute yoga classes each week, and another had participants attend daily one-hour yoga classes.

Stephanie Faubion, MD, Director for the Mayo Clinic Center for Women’s Health and Medical Director for The Menopause Society, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that this was a relatively small body of evidence. “While physical activity is an important component of a healthy lifestyle during midlife, I would be cautious about interpreting these findings to mean that exercise is a treatment for depression related specifically to menopause,” she said.

Research has shown that physical activity can positively affect mental health. Studies have also found that regular exercise can help improve symptoms of depression and anxiety.

Faubion told Healthline that, broadly speaking, regular physical activity may support mood through multiple pathways, including better sleep, improved physical function, and overall well-being.

However, she also noted that this study cannot tell us precisely why the improvements occurred or whether aerobic exercise is superior to other forms of activity.

Faubion said that recommending physical activity during and after menopause extends well beyond mood.

“Physical activity is important for cardiovascular and metabolic health, maintaining muscle mass and physical function, and supporting bone health,” she said.

“These become particularly important at midlife as women experience age- and menopause-related changes in body composition, bone, and cardiometabolic health,” Faubion added.

Ross agreed that physical activity is important for more than just mood and mental health improvement. She also noted that there are other types of exercise beyond ABIs and MBAs that can benefit people during menopause:

“These types of activities help with weight loss or allow women to maintain a healthy weight. If you are not ready for aerobic exercises, stretching and simple exercises help with balance and stability,” Ross said.

Faubion told Healthline that physical activity is an important part of healthy aging and should be encouraged during the menopause transition, but it should not be suggested that women can simply exercise their way out of significant depression or other bothersome menopause symptoms.

“Women experiencing persistent depression, anxiety, or symptoms that interfere with their quality of life should seek evaluation and discuss the full range of evidence-based treatment options with their healthcare clinician,” Faubion said.

#4695. Tesla wins trade zone status for Texas Megapacks, but China tariffs stay

Tesla’s Megapack factory in Brookshire, Texas, is now officially a foreign-trade zone, a US customs program that lets manufacturers defer duties on imported parts. The FTZ Board’s approval, published in the Federal Register on Monday, runs for 14 months.

It’s easy to read this as Tesla getting a pass on tariffs for the Chinese LFP cells inside its Megapacks. Tesla’s own application says otherwise: parts hit by Section 301, 232, or 122 tariffs still pay them.

Tesla filed the request on May 20 for Subzone 84AM, part of FTZ 84 in the Houston area. That’s the factory where Tesla started Megapack 3 production in August, with a planned capacity of 50 GWh per year.

The application lists roughly 80 imported components Tesla wants to bring in under zone procedures, from coolant pumps and transformers to busbars, wiring harnesses, circuit boards and battery cells. Duty rates on those parts go up to 6.5%, while finished Megapacks and Bento inverters range from duty-free to 3.4%.

That gap is the usual reason companies set up an FTZ. A manufacturer in a zone can normally elect to pay the finished product’s lower rate instead of the rate on each imported part.

But the application spells out the limit. Components subject to duties under Section 122 of the Trade Act, Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act, or Section 301 “require subject merchandise to be admitted to FTZs in privileged foreign status,” according to the notice.

Privileged foreign status locks in a part’s own classification and tariff treatment when it enters the zone. So a Chinese LFP cell that ends up in a Megapack sold in the US still pays the Section 301 tariff on Chinese non-EV lithium-ion batteries, which jumped from 7.5% to 25% on January 1, 2026. Tesla just pays it later, when the finished Megapack leaves the zone.

Here’s what Tesla actually gets out of it:

The approval came with the same wording the FTZ Board has used all year. Production was “authorized on a limited basis,” and “further subject to a fourteen-month time period.”

Tesla got an identical decision for Megapack and inverter production at Fremont, Livermore and Lathrop in California this summer, with a one-year limit instead. Eastman Chemical, battery pack maker Rose Batteries, and chipmaker Qorvo all received similar time-limited, “limited basis” approvals in 2026.

The 14-month clock puts the expiry around the end of 2027. That’s roughly when LG Energy Solution is due to start supplying Tesla with LFP cells from Michigan under a $4.3 billion contract for Megapack 3, with mass production expected in the second half of 2027.

Tesla hasn’t hidden the issue. When tariffs escalated in April 2025, CFO Vaibhav Taneja said the impact on energy storage would be “outsized since we source lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells from China.” We wrote at the time that Tesla’s only growing business was kneecapped by Trump’s tariffs.

Tesla has since brought up its own LFP cell factory in Nevada, but Taneja said it would only cover a fraction of Tesla’s installed capacity. And Brookshire alone is designed for 50 GWh a year, on top of the 40 GWh Lathrop factory in California.

Tesla’s Megapacks are bringing big batteries to the grid, but you can get the same benefits at home by pairing solar with storage. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4694. EcoFlow’s new DELTA Gen4 portable power stations keep a reserve of extra power for emergencies

Published Nov 4, 2026 1:24 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

If you’ve ever driven with white knuckles to a gas station while your car’s range read “0 miles,” you’ll appreciate a new feature on this portable power station. EcoFlow is building a similar cushion into its new DELTA Gen4 portable power stations. A feature called Emergency Power Mode holds back a small reserve for charging phones after the screen hits 0 percent.

Two models are on sale today through EcoFlow’s website: the DELTA 3000 Gen4 at an early-bird $1,299 and the DELTA 3800 Gen4 at $1,699, against list prices of $1,699 and $2,199. Both put out 3,600 watts in chassis EcoFlow says are smaller and lighter than its DELTA 3 Ultra models, which include the DELTA 3 Ultra Plus we tried last year. They arrive a month after EcoFlow’s TITAN home batteries targeted whole-home backup.

A power station spends some charge just keeping its inverter awake. EcoFlow rates both DELTA Gen4 models at 14 watts with the AC outlets switched on and nothing plugged in, and 3 watts in standby. At 14 watts, a full day of idling uses 336 watt-hours, about 11 percent of the DELTA 3000 Gen4’s 3,072Wh battery.

The 3-watt standby number is what lets EcoFlow claim a fully charged DELTA 3800 Gen4 can sit for about 52 days before it drains, which matters for one parked in a closet waiting for an outage. EcoFlow pairs the lower overhead with a mode called Fridge Runtime Boost and rates the DELTA 3000 Gen4 for up to 58 hours of refrigerator runtime. The DELTA 3800 Gen4 gets more than 70 hours.

Those fridge numbers come from EcoFlow’s own tests with an empty 654-liter Samsung refrigerator, and the company notes that food load, room temperature, and door openings all change the result. The mode also supports one compressor-based appliance, such as a fridge or freezer, at a time, and EcoFlow says not to run other AC loads alongside it. We haven’t tested either DELTA Gen4 model yet, so these performance figures are EcoFlow’s. Emergency Power Mode covers what’s left after the battery runs down. You turn it on from the unit or the EcoFlow app, and EcoFlow says the reserve can give an iPhone 17 nearly a full extra charge.

Both DELTA Gen4 models share a 16.8 x 11.4-inch footprint, and both are rated for 3,600 watts continuous and 7,200 watts of surge from their 120V outlets. That’s enough to run a 1,500-watt space heater and a refrigerator at the same time with room to spare. EcoFlow’s original DELTA Pro weighed about 99 pounds to hit the same 3,600-watt rating.

The DELTA 3800 Gen4 fits 691 extra watt-hours and about 10 more pounds into the same footprint, for 3,763Wh at 67.5 pounds. EcoFlow says that’s roughly 33 pounds lighter than the DELTA Pro, and it holds slightly more energy. The DELTA 3000 Gen4 holds 3,072Wh at 57.3 pounds, and EcoFlow puts it at about 20 percent lighter than the DELTA 3 Ultra, with the same capacity.

The bigger model also has more ways to grow. The DELTA 3800 Gen4 takes up to 2,000 watts of solar across two inputs and has an expansion port for up to two extra batteries, including the DELTA Pro 3 Smart Extra Battery, for about 12kWh total. The DELTA 3000 Gen4 has one 1,000-watt solar input, and its spec sheet lists no battery port.

EcoFlow says the DELTA 3000 Gen4 refills from a wall outlet in under two hours and the DELTA 3800 Gen4 in under 2.5 hours. The 3kWh, 3,600-watt class is crowded, with Anker’s SOLIX F3000 and Jackery’s Explorer 3000 v2 at the same capacity and output. Our guide to the best portable power stations covers the field.

The DELTA 3000 Gen4 and DELTA 3800 Gen4 are listed for preorder. As of November 4, EcoFlow shows the DELTA 3800 Gen4 shipping in late November and the DELTA 3000 Gen4 in early December.

EcoFlow’s early-bird pricing runs through December 7. That puts the DELTA 3800 Gen4 at $1,699, 23 percent off its $2,199 list, and the DELTA 3000 Gen4 at $1,299, which is $400 below its $1,699 list.

For a house that needs a fridge, a router, and a few lamps through a weekend outage, this is the DELTA to look at first. It has the same 3,600-watt output as its bigger sibling and weighs about 10 pounds less. The savings come out of expandability, since it gets one 1,000-watt solar input, four charging methods, and no listed battery expansion.

At early-bird prices, $400 more buys 691 extra watt-hours, a second 1,000-watt solar input, and an expansion port that takes the system to about 12kWh with add-on batteries. That port is the reason to step up if you plan to expand a home-backup system later. EcoFlow rates it for more than 70 hours on a refrigerator and lists six ways to charge it.

#4693. Kia racks up another record month as its new $30K electric SUV hits dealers

Kia is eyeing its fourth consecutive annual US sales record after another record-breaking October. With the new 2027 EV3 arriving, Kia is “confident” the momentum will carry into Q4 and well into 2027.

“With six consecutive months of record-breaking sales, Kia is accelerating toward a fourth straight annual sales record,” Kia America vice president of sales Eric Watson said on Tuesday.

Kia sold 80,008 vehicles in the US last month, up 16% year over year and marking its best October sales month ever.

Kia said electrified and hybrid vehicles drove the growth, with sales up 112% and 114% YOY, both setting new sales records.

Several Kia models posted strong YOY sales growth, including the three-row electric EV9 (+111%), Telluride (+63%), EV6 (+58%), Seltos (+43%), Sorento (+31%), Carnival (+17%), K4 (+14%), and Sportage (+12%).

Regarding its fully electric vehicles. Sales of the EV9, Kia’s three-row electric SUV, are now up 5% year-to-date, with 13,835 units sold through October.

Although EV6 sales rebounded slightly last month, they are still down 39% YTD, with 7,067 units sold through October.

Kia’s new entry-level electric SUV, the EV3 (check out our review), is now in showrooms nationwide. After it went on sale in mid-August, Kia sold 1,496 EV3s in its first two months.

The 2027 EV3 is Kia’s most affordable fully electric vehicle, starting at $29,890. That’s for the base EV3 Light model, which uses a 58.3 kWh battery that provides up to 221 miles of range.

Higher-priced trims, including the Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT, use an 81.4 kWh battery for up to 321 miles of range.

Front-wheel-drive (FWD) models have a single 201-horsepower electric motor. Upgrading to all-wheel-drive (AWD) costs $3,200 and adds a rear electric motor for a combined 261 horsepower.

#4692. Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Increase Dementia, Stroke Risk

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Your hub for heart health management, insights, and solutions

Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.

UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations. This category of foods includes packaged snack foods, sugary cereals, soft drinks, and frozen ready-to-eat meals.

UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

Previous research has linked these foods to adverse cardiometabolic outcomes. This new study adds to growing evidence linking high UPF intake to adverse health outcomes.

This was a cross-sectional analysis of 8,783 adults between the ages of 35 and 69 without cardiovascular disease. The participants were all enrolled in the Canadian Alliance for Healthy Hearts and Minds (CAHHM) and Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiology-MIND (PURE-MIND) cohorts.

The researchers used MRI scans to evaluate the participants’ brains. They also set out to analyze the cross-sectional relationship between UPF consumption, body fat, vascular brain injury (VBI), and cognitive performance.

They measured the participants’ habitual UPF intake using a food frequency questionnaire. Intake was expressed as servings based on a 2,000-calorie-per-day diet.

UPFs accounted for an average of 25% of participants’ daily diets. For the individuals with the highest intake, this increased to 45% of everything on their plates, compared to 16% for those who ate the least.

The researchers also noted that UPFs were not just an added part of individual diets. These foods appeared to replace whole foods.

Among people with the highest UPF intake, fruits, vegetables, grains, and other minimally processed foods accounted for 41% of their daily food intake. Among those with the lowest UPF intake, minimally processed foods made up 68% of their daily intake.

When the researchers compared the highest intake to the lowest, they found that those with a higher intake of UPFs had 1.7% more body fat. They also found that people with a higher UPF intake had higher odds of VBI.

“These findings are concerning, but it is important to remember that an association does not prove cause and effect,” said Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“From my perspective as a preventive cardiology dietitian, these findings reinforce the importance of nourishing our blood vessels to support both cardiovascular and brain health.”

Although researchers found no significant differences in cognitive performance, the signs of vascular brain injury observed in the study have been associated with an increased risk of stroke and cognitive decline.

These findings suggest a possible link between UPF intake and signs of brain changes. However, participants were only assessed once and weren’t followed over time. This means the researchers were unable to determine whether UPFs directly caused the changes.

“While we can’t conclude from this study that limiting UPFs would improve brain health, we have decades of literature demonstrating that higher intakes of green leafy vegetables, brightly colored fruits, whole grains, and lean protein sources are good for brain health,” said Suzanne Judd, PhD, Director of the UC College of Medicine’s Center for Public Health, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“So focusing more on what can be brought into the diet rather than what should be eliminated might be a good way to start,” she added.

The preservatives [in UPFs] may have a direct impact on the vascular system, while the loss of antioxidants results in a less robust response to inflammation in the body.

“Additionally, sugar or salt is often added to make the food a bit tastier so people consume it in higher quantities. Over-consumption of food can lead to weight gain and diabetes, which can negatively impact brain health,” Judd said.

Judd told Healthline that it is virtually impossible to completely avoid UPFs. Even some “health” foods, like protein powder and some yogurts, are considered ultra-processed.

It is more important to look at diet overall and emphasize consuming foods as close to their natural state as possible, such as fruits, vegetables, grains, and meats purchased raw or frozen and then cooked at home.

Routhenstein recommended starting simply with one manageable swap rather than trying to overhaul your entire diet.

She said that you should identify an ultra-processed food you eat regularly and consider a more nutrient-rich alternative. It is important to account for convenience, food preferences, budget, and lifestyle so that the change feels realistic and is sustainable over the long term.

“I want people to feel empowered, not fearful, when making food choices,” said Routhenstein. “Healthy eating does not mean having to cook everything from scratch. What matters most is building consistent, nourishing habits that support both heart and brain health.”

#4691. California has way more bugs than we thought

Published Nov 4, 2026 2:00 PM EST

It’s true that there are more insects on Earth than any other animal. They make up roughly 80 percent of the planet’s animals and include about 900,000 known species. However, those jaw-dropping numbers can make it easy to undercount our six-legged friends. Take the state of California. Over 60,000 different species of insects reside in the Golden State, and scientists have only described about two-thirds of them. A study published today in the journal Ecography details the findings, which represents a huge bump in the estimated number of insects in California.

The study is part of the California Insect Barcode Initiative (CIBI), a $6 million project to collect and identify every species of insect in the state. Multiple institutions including the California Department of Food and Agriculture, UC Berkeley, UC Riverside, San Diego Natural History Museum, the California Academy of Sciences in San Francisco, and Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County (NHM) worked together to DNA barcode over one million insect specimens.

To build the insect library, the team gathered tissue samples from museum collections and caught living insects in 72 ecoregions around the state. Ecoregions are places that have similar ecosystems as defined by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). They also undertook research expeditions to 454 additional locations across California, and used Malaise traps to gather the insects. Malaise traps passively capture bugs, but require a bit of work to maintain.

“This is an example of community science. Volunteers stepped forward to help with sampling by managing traps, which we would not have been able to do for continuous weekly sampling,” Giar-Ann Kung, a study co-author and NHM Entomology collections manager, said in a statement.

The study looked at Level 3 ecoregions, which include places like the Mojave Basin and Range, Southern California Mountains, and Sierra Nevada. They found that the Mojave Basin and Range have the highest insect species richness.

The team also compared parallel ecoregions and found that each one is home to its own unique mix of insect life, even if they have a similar climate and geography. While there are parallels between locations within the same ecoregion, the team found that the richness of life across California is more abundant and more delicate than previously thought. Researchers say that these results highlight the need for more aggressive conservation of California’s wild places to protect the insects living there.

#4690. This electric microcar just got a 50 mph upgrade, plus a secret Turbo mode

The adorable little Eli ZERO electric microcar is growing up. At this year’s EICMA motorcycle show in Milan, Eli Electric Vehicles is unveiling a faster, more powerful version of its pint-sized electric car, along with a sporty new limited-edition model that even includes a hidden Turbo mode.

First teased last week, the new Eli ZERO MX is the company’s first L7e-class electric vehicle, allowing it to reach speeds of up to 80 km/h (50 mph). That’s a significant jump from the 45 km/h (28 mph) top speed of the original L6e version that we originally reviewed, opening the door to a much wider range of driving scenarios.

And perhaps most importantly, the company managed to squeeze that extra performance into the same tiny package.

The Eli ZERO MX retains the original’s ultra-compact 2.25-meter (7.4-foot) length, making it considerably smaller than even the smallest conventional passenger cars.

But under that tiny exterior, the MX now packs up to 20 kW (27 hp) of peak power, compared to the 12 kW (16 hp) of the original Eli ZERO.

The upgraded model also features a 14.4 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery, providing a claimed range of up to 200 km (124 miles) per charge.

That’s a pretty respectable figure for a vehicle designed primarily for short urban and suburban trips.

The rear-wheel-drive microcar features selectable ECO and SPORT driving modes, a 30% climbing capability, and a tight 7.2-meter turning circle. Charging is handled by a 3.3 kW onboard charger, allowing owners to plug in at home or use public AC charging stations.

Despite its diminutive size, the Eli ZERO MX also includes a surprisingly long list of features normally associated with much larger cars.

Those include air conditioning and heating, a panoramic moonroof, soft-close doors, keyless entry and start, electric power steering, ABS, front and rear disc brakes, and an electronic parking brake.

There’s also an 8.8-inch digital instrument cluster, a reversing camera with rear radar, and an optional 10.1-inch infotainment display with Apple CarPlay.

The MX is available in four colors: Pearl White, Arctic Silver, Graphite, and Champagne.

The biggest difference, though, is the vehicle’s classification. While the original Eli ZERO falls under Europe’s L6e light quadricycle category, the new MX qualifies as an L7e heavy quadricycle. That means it generally requires a higher-level driving license, but also allows for considerably more performance.

For drivers who love the idea of a tiny electric runabout but need something capable of keeping up with faster suburban traffic, the MX could be a much more compelling option.

Eli isn’t stopping at a faster version of its microcar.

The company is also introducing the Eli ZERO Race Edition, a limited-production model available in both the original L6e and the new L7e configurations.

Finished in an exclusive Turbo Red paint job, the Race Edition features racing stripes across the hood, roof, and body panels, along with a rear spoiler and special wheel badging.

Inside, the sporty treatment continues with a two-tone Race Red microsuede and light gray interior, including special upholstery, dashboard accents, and embroidered seats.

But the most interesting feature isn’t immediately visible.

Eli has included a secret Turbo mode activated by pressing and holding the hazard light button. After four quick chimes, the digital instrument cluster switches to Turbo mode and the car’s acceleration response becomes sharper.

Importantly, the feature doesn’t increase the vehicle’s top speed or exceed its regulatory performance limits. Instead, it changes the way the car responds to accelerator inputs, giving it a sportier driving feel.

It’s a fun little Easter egg in a vehicle that already has plenty of personality.

Eli is also offering a new Carbon Aero Kit, consisting of a carbon fiber front splitter, side skirts, and rear wing. The kit is compatible with both the Race Edition and other Eli ZERO models.

Eli has spent years developing its vision of a smaller, lighter, and more efficient alternative to conventional cars, particularly for the short trips that make up much of our daily driving.

The company has already launched its second-generation Eli ZERO, which shares the same 96V electrical architecture and aluminum chassis as the new MX.

By expanding into the L7e category, Eli is addressing one of the biggest limitations of its original design: speed.

A 28 mph (45 km/h) microcar makes plenty of sense in dense urban centers, but its usefulness quickly drops off when drivers need to venture onto faster roads. A 50 mph (80 km/h) version, on the other hand, could make the same tiny vehicle practical for considerably more people.

In the US, this could go pretty much anywhere that didn't require highway driving. Perfect one-and-a-halfth car.

The Eli ZERO family is currently available through authorized dealers in several European markets, including Italy, Norway, and the Netherlands, with prices starting at €10,500 (approximately US $12,000) for the base model. Pricing for the new MX and Race Edition hasn’t yet been announced.

Eli also has a pilot program underway in the United States, though the new models are being introduced primarily for the European market.

Both the Eli ZERO MX and Race Edition will be on display at EICMA 2026 in Milan from November 3–8.

For a vehicle that takes up less than half the space of a conventional car, the Eli ZERO is certainly finding ways to make a bigger impression!

#4689. Why Real Paintings Can Look AI-Generated

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Take a look at the two moonlit scenes below. One was painted in 1839. The other was generated by artificial intelligence (AI) in 2026. Which one would you choose as being the work of a human artist?

Before looking for the answer, consider what guided your choice. The light? The details? Perhaps one looks a little too polished, while the other feels more natural. How confident are you that those qualities tell you who made it?

I find this question interesting because it asks us to examine something we might otherwise take for granted: what human creativity is supposed to look like.

In a preliminary, unpublished study, I asked 202 U.S. adults to judge images drawn from five 19th-century paintings and five AI-generated versions of the same scenes. Each participant saw five images, presented individually in random order, and identified each as human-made, AI-generated, or something they were unsure about.

Among the 920 answers that named a source, participants were correct about 45 percent of the time. For these images, that was below the 50 percent expected from a coin flip.

But the direction of the mistakes was more interesting. Participants labeled the original paintings as AI-generated 51 percent of the time. They gave that label to the actual AI images only 42 percent of the time. The original looked more artificial than its AI counterpart in four of the five pairs.

And the answer to the opening question? Image A is Johan Christian Dahl’s View of Dresden by Moonlight, painted in 1839. Image B is AI-generated. Among definite answers, 69 percent labeled Dahl’s painting AI, compared with 51 percent for the generated version.

This reversal has a parallel in poetry. Brian Porter and Edouard Machery found that nonexpert readers were more likely to attribute AI-generated poems to humans than poems actually written by established poets (2024). Our expectations about human expression can apparently lead us away from the humans.

Why might this happen? Participants’ explanations offered a clue. Nearly a quarter mentioned a polished or “too perfect” appearance as a sign of AI. That seems like a reasonable suspicion until we consider how much effort painters have devoted to achieving precisely those qualities.

Consider the still life below. The original is Image B, painted by Severin Roesen in 1852. Its elaborate arrangement and luminous fruit might fit someone’s idea of what an image generator produces. Yet here those qualities belong to a human painter.

One possible explanation is what psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman called the representativeness heuristic: judging something by how closely it resembles our idea of a category (1974). If our mental picture of AI art is smooth, detailed, and beautifully lit, a painting with those features may seem machine-made. (This is an interpretation of the findings; the study did not experimentally establish that polish caused the mistakes.)

Experience offered little reassurance. Regular users of AI image tools were less likely to answer “not sure,” but showed no detectable accuracy advantage. Being comfortable making a judgment and being correct about it are separate matters.

Of course, five painting pairs cannot tell us how people judge all art. Participants viewed digital reproductions, and each made only five judgments. The results do not establish that expertise is useless or that nobody can detect AI. They do suggest that familiar visual clues can mislead us in this particular setting.

That matters because authorship can change appreciation. In experiments by Lucas Bellaiche and colleagues, artworks received more favorable evaluations when labeled human-created rather than AI-created, even though all the images were generated by AI (2023). The story we attach to an image can become part of what we see in it.

What gives me pause is the possibility that we might dismiss human skill precisely because it looks accomplished. Before treating an image as obviously artificial, I would want to know more about where it came from.

Dahl painted that moonlit scene in 1839. The suspicion that it looks like AI belongs entirely to us.

Porter, B., & Machery, E. (2024). AI-generated poetry is indistinguishable from human-written poetry and is rated more favorably. Scientific Reports, 14, 26133. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-76900-1

Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases. Science, 185(4157), 1124–1131. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124

Bellaiche, L., Shahi, R., Turpin, M. H., Ragnhildstveit, A., Sprockett, S., Barr, N., Christensen, A., & Seli, P. (2023). Humans versus AI: Whether and why we prefer human-created compared to AI-created artwork. Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications, 8, 42. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41235-023-00499-6

#4688. A Handful of Pistachios May Help You Sleep Better, Review Says

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?

A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.

Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.

While the findings suggest that pistachios may support sleep, the evidence is inconclusive and warrants further study.

“Pistachios are compelling for sleep research because they bring together several nutrients and plant compounds connected to sleep physiology within one whole food,” said study author Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research in the Department of Medicine at Columbia University Institute of Nutrition, in a news release.

“Rather than focusing on a single ‘sleep nutrient,’ this review provides a rationale for studying how the complete pistachio food matrix may affect sleep-related pathways,” she continued.

The narrative review examined existing research on pistachios and sleep-related biology.

The researchers explored whether the combination of nutrients in pistachios could promote quality sleep.

Rather than identifying pistachios as a sleep remedy, the researchers outlined biological pathways through which their nutrients and bioactive compounds might influence sleep.

“We were particularly interested in pistachios because they are particularly high in phytomelatonin, polyphenols, and carotenoids, which we noted were plant-derived components that had been shown to have sleep benefits in preclinical studies,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“We also noted their high content of tryptophan and vitamin B6, which are relevant to melatonin production in humans,” she continued.

Pistachios contain several nutrients associated with sleep, including melatonin, which helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.

Other studies examining the effects of some of these nutrients on sleep offer further context.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of tryptophan supplementation found that it may reduce wakefulness after sleep onset, particularly at doses of at least 1 gram (g) daily. However, an ounce of pistachios supplies only about 71 mg, which is much less than the doses examined by the researchers.

Additionally, a 2023 review of dietary polyphenols led by St-Onge identified potential links between plant compounds and sleep outcomes, although results varied across studies.

Neither review established that polyphenols or tryptophan from pistachios specifically affected sleep quality.

“I was not surprised that pistachios may help support sleep, given their combination of nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” said Michelle Routhenstein, MS, a preventive cardiology dietitian at EntirelyNourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“Pistachios provide tryptophan, an amino acid the body uses to produce serotonin and melatonin; vitamin B6, which supports these pathways; and magnesium, which plays a role in nervous system function and sleep regulation,” she told Healthline.

The new review highlights the concept of the “food matrix,” or how nutrients and bioactive compounds interact within a whole food.

Instead of investigating tryptophan, magnesium, or melatonin individually, researchers were curious about the combined effects of consuming them together in pistachios.

Laboratory and simulated-digestion research offers clues about how fiber and plant compounds in pistachios and peanuts interact with gut microbes. However, these findings do not establish that eating pistachios changes sleep quality in real-world conditions.

Broader nutrition research also points to a relationship between diet and sleep.

A 2021 review in the Annual Review of Nutrition examined evidence linking dietary patterns and individual nutrients to sleep outcomes. The findings suggest a relationship between sleep and diet, but note that more research is needed to determine cause and effect.

In a nutshell, the current evidence builds a compelling case for pistachios as a sleep aid.

However, it’s too soon to recommend pistachios as a sleep remedy, as many factors may affect sleep quality and insomnia.

“Sleep difficulties can have different underlying causes,” Routhenstein noted. “If inadequate intake of these nutrients is a contributing factor, pistachios may help, but they may not address sleep issues related to other nutrient deficiencies or other causes.”

Much of the supporting evidence cited in the review comes from studies of individual nutrients, other foods, laboratory experiments, or biological mechanisms rather than from trials involving whole pistachios.

Researchers have also reported significant variations in the melatonin content of pistachios, making the amount in a typical serving difficult to pinpoint.

Additionally, the review received support from American Pistachio Growers, and the corresponding author, St-Onge, serves on its advisory board. Larger studies and clinical trials are needed, ideally without industry funding, to ensure well-rounded results.

Indeed, the authors call for randomized controlled trials examining whether eating pistachios affects sleep outcomes, including sleep quality, duration, and melatonin levels.

“This was a review; we noted that the complete profile of pistachios would make them well-suited to support healthful sleep, but research is needed to evaluate this,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“This is the next step, and something we are actively working on. We also need to better understand what dosage and frequency of consumption would be optimal.”

Regardless, a handful of pistachios is still considered a healthy choice as part of a balanced diet.

“A small handful, about 1 ounce of shelled pistachios, is an appropriate portion,” Routhenstein said. “Enjoy them during the day or as a light afternoon or evening snack when you’re hungry.”

If nutrients like tryptophan help promote sleep, it’s possible that other nuts could yield similar results.

“Other nuts, such as almonds and walnuts, may offer similar benefits because they also contain nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” Routhenstein said.

“Early research is encouraging, but it’s too soon to say how much they might help.”

Other foods, like turkey, also contain tryptophan.

“For someone allergic to nuts, foods such as tofu, beans, oats, eggs, dairy, and fish can provide tryptophan, which the body uses to make serotonin and melatonin,” Routhenstein said. “The goal is to meet their nutrient needs rather than rely on one food to improve sleep.”

Sleep health depends on multiple factors. As such, Routhenstein recommends a personalized approach to getting better sleep, from what you eat and when you eat to addressing any nutritional gaps.

“I would also encourage regular, balanced meals throughout the day to support blood sugar management, especially for those with diabetes, while avoiding large meals close to bedtime,” Routhenstein said. “Caffeine later in the day and alcohol in the evening are also worth considering as possible sleep disruptors.”
